title: California scientist wins a Nobel Prize, then makes school lunches for his kids
summary: Dr. Karl Deisseroth spent hours fielding congratulatory calls after learning that he had won a Nobel Prize for medicine for helping to open a new field of brain science called optogenetics
story: Dr. Karl Deisseroth spent hours fielding congratulatory calls after learning that he had won a Nobel Prize for medicine for helping to open a new field of brain science called optogenetics

STANFORD, Calif. -- Dr. Karl Deisseroth spent hours fielding congratulatory calls after learning early Monday that he had won a Nobel Prize for medicine for helping to open a new field of brain science called optogenetics.

But it wasn't long before the California scientist asked for a break from all the attention for a more ordinary task: He needed to make school lunches for his children, who were asleep in the family home in Stanford, where their father had been speaking in the middle of the night with journalists and well-wishers.
Deisseroth, 54, shared this year’s medicine prize with two researchers in Germany for their work in optogenetics, a field that combines light with genes to switch on and off neurons in living brains.

A self-described night owl, the Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator and Stanford University professor often works past midnight. After reviewing papers and emailing his students, he said he had just gone to lie down when he got the call from the Nobel Assembly in Stockholm.
“I almost felt as if I’d lost the power of forming words,” he told The Associated Press, “but I recovered after a minute or two.”
He regained speech quickly enough for remote interviews with AP science reporters. Speedy emails with the Stanford communications staff had helped put them in touch.
“No real sleep was achieved,” he said an hour after the announcement.
As the science reporters chatted with Deisseroth over the phone and Zoom, an AP photographer and videographer raced to his home in Stanford.

The photographer arrived around 3:30 a.m. to find Halloween decorations outside the home but just one light on inside. He was worried he had the wrong house before mustering the courage to knock on the door.
Dr. Michelle Monje-Deisseroth, the scientist's wife, answered and ushered the photographer into their home, where the Nobel winner was taking calls from the couch.

Monje-Deisseroth, an HHMI investigator and Stanford pediatric neuro-oncologist, was at his side when she wasn’t making coffee for the Stanford communications staff who had joined the celebration. Deisseroth was surprised to hear his work had been honored with a Nobel Prize, he told the AP, but his wife was not.
Deisseroth recounted the research he conducted with fellow Nobel winners Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, and its real-world impact.

“For me, I’m a physician-scientist. I am a psychiatrist. I care about patients and my patients who have autism, who have depression,” he said. “I care about the hope that this brings. But I’m also a basic scientist, and I care about understanding this amazing organ, the brain, and how it works and how it integrates and computes and delivers all the things that make us human.”

As Deisseroth wrapped up the interviews, he told the Stanford staff he needed an hourlong break beginning at 6:30 a.m. His kids would be waking up, he said, and they would need lunches before leaving for school.
When one of the Stanford representatives wondered if the neighbors would mind all the late-night commotion, Monje-Deisseroth shrugged it off.
They live in faculty housing, she said. There are a lot of Nobels in the neighborhood.
Ramakrishnan reported from New York. Associated Press writers Stefanie Dazio in Berlin and Lauran Neergaard in Washington contributed to this report.

title: AI industry insiders voice alarms to NYC council as local governments take up safety concerns
summary: Artificial intelligence insiders are warning New York City’s leaders about dangers of the emerging technology, calling for greater oversight as local governments move to respond to mounting safety concerns
story: Artificial intelligence insiders are warning New York City’s leaders about dangers of the emerging technology, calling for greater oversight as local governments move to respond to mounting safety concerns

NEW YORK -- Artificial intelligence insiders warned New York City's leaders about the dangers of the emerging technology on Monday, calling for greater oversight as local governments move to respond to mounting concerns that the systems could endanger humanity.

At a hearing of the New York City Council, recently departed employees of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind described a reckless culture at the firms, saying the biggest tech companies are racing to create technology they do not understand how to control.

“The companies run on a startup mindset: Move fast, break things, fix them later. That works for a photo sharing app. It does not work for building the most powerful technology ever built," said Jacob Coxon, a former engineer at Anthropic who has become a leading voice for regulation.

State and city governments have been considering ways to regulate AI as the Trump administration has taken a passive approach and Congress has proven inactive. President Donald Trump has dismissed AI fears as a “hoax” and signed an agreement late last month that spells out a series of voluntary steps for the companies to take and largely allows them to self-police.

Coxon was a little-known engineer at Anthropic until he announced his departure through a series of social media posts that caught global attention. He told the Council that AI could have tremendous upsides, but without transparency and safeguards, it's more likely that things will spiral out of control.
“On the current path, I think it is more likely than not that humanity loses control to these AIs and it could end in human extinction,” Coxon said.

Days after Coxon resigned and aired his fears of worst-case scenarios, top executives including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk said they agreed AI’s development needs to slow down. AI companies have detailed steps they have taken to prioritize safety, but a coordinated industry slowdown faces several obstacles.

A panel of AI company staffers — representing tech giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta — also testified at the hearing in Manhattan on Monday, telling officials that their systems are already improving people's daily lives and stressing that they are laser-focused on safety.
Anthropic and OpenAI have said their advanced AI products need to be regulated, and company representatives at the hearing expressed openness to some of the Council's suggestions.
“I share your commitment to ensuring that technology is developed safely and that its benefits are widely shared,” said Morgan Dwyer of OpenAI.
At one point during the hearing, Julie Menin, the speaker of the City Council, asked each of the company representatives to “quantify the risk posed by AI in the worst case catastrophic scenario.”

Dwyer answered: “I don’t know — I also don’t think it matters whether it’s 1% or 10% or 20% chance that something catastrophic will go wrong. None of these levels is remotely acceptable. We should not train models that we cannot make an extremely strong case that we can keep under human control."
Menin slammed the response as “flippant at best."
“I would say that the percentage chance doesn’t matter. What matters is the commitment to safety, and that is what OpenAI is committed to doing," Dwyer said.

The City Council is considering several AI regulations, including proposals to require companies to disclose information about AI tools, require third-party approval for AI systems in the city and allow whistleblowers to receive a portion of fines from AI companies that violate laws.

Separately, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, has moved to impose reporting and transparency standards around AI, as have governors elsewhere, though their power is somewhat limited since AI technology can reach across state lines, as well as the globe.
Logan Graham, of Anthropic, told the Council the company welcomes “smart regulation" and that state and local governments have a role to play in developing frameworks.
“AI is powerful enough that getting this wrong has real consequences, for individuals, institutions, public trust," he said. “We have to work relentlessly to do the science of mitigating the risks.”

title: Lack of transparency in what space weapons nations are pursuing and even on what's already in orbit
summary: The United States military recently confirmed that the U.S. has deployed weapons in space
story: The United States military recently confirmed that the U.S. has deployed weapons in space

VIENNA -- Air Force Secretary Troy Meink made headlines recently by confirming the United States has deployed weapons in space. He did not, however, detail what the weapons were, how they work or if they were targeting other objects in space.
It’s not just U.S. efforts regarding space weapons that remain shrouded in mystery.
Here's a look at issues that concern experts:

Meink, speaking at a defense conference, said the U.S. has fielded “on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action,” referring to U.S. forces. It remains unclear which type of weapon Meink was referencing.

Such resources as the 2026 Global Counterspace Capabilities Report, published by the nonprofit Secure World Foundation and based on publicly available information, help provide an overview of potential space weapons.
The report lists five categories of counterspace capabilities. It examines systems being developed by 13 countries, among them the U.S., Russia, China, India, Australia, France, Iran, and Israel.

These include satellites designed to maneuver near, inspect, disable, or destroy spacecraft. The report also examines ground, air, or sea-launched missile interceptors designed to destroy satellites kinetically.

Furthermore, the report highlights electronic warfare, such as jamming, in addition to lasers or high-power microwaves meant to blind or damage satellite sensors. The report also lists cyber operations targeting space networks.

Victoria Samson, chief director of space security and stability at the foundation, which advocates for the peaceful use of space, said the existence of various satellites and their physical location in orbit is fairly transparent but their capabilities and intended uses are harder to understand.

For example, the Vienna-based U.N. Office for Outer Space Affairs supports transparency in space by maintaining a register which links each object to its responsible country. States who signed on to a 1976 agreement are required to provide information on launches by governments and private companies as well as the general function of the space object, but are not required to provide details on their purpose.

As an example of something that could be used for both military and non-military purposes, it became known in 2021 that China had tested a satellite with a robotic arm that can maneuver to a system, grab it, and move it out of orbit. In 2022, China used such a system for the first time to tow one of its dead satellites out of orbit.
Furthermore, the U.S. warned two years ago that Russia was developing a new space-based, anti-satellite weapon, though the White House said the danger wasn’t imminent at the time.
Then-White House national security spokesman John Kirby declined to comment on whether the weapon was nuclear capable, but did say it would violate the Outer Space Treaty.
Russia denied developing such a new capability.

The Outer Space Treaty is the main international agreement that establishes the rules and norms for how countries explore and use space. In addition to Russia, the U.S., China and all other nuclear-armed nations are party to the treaty.

Article IV states that parties “undertake not to place in orbit around the earth any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, install such weapons on celestial bodies, or station such weapons in outer space in any other manner.”
The treaty also declares that space is a global commons that can be used for only peaceful purposes.
The treaty was concluded in 1967 during the Cold War when the U.S. and the Soviet Union were both racing to explore space, and conducted a series of nuclear tests in orbit.
At the time, space looked radically different.
Jonathan McDowell, a retired astronomer from the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, has been tracking satellite launches for more than four decades.

By the end of 1967, 128 satellites were in orbit and communicating with Earth, according to McDowell. At the time, all satellites were the product of state-backed, public projects. This is compared to what McDowell says are approximately 16,810 functioning satellites today — many of which are from companies such as SpaceX’s Starlink network.

In 1962, the U.S. exploded a series of atomic bombs in space as part of Operation Fishbowl. The first one, the Starfish Prime test, was launched from an atoll southwest of Hawaii. The explosion caused an artificial radiation belt that destroyed several satellites and partially knocked out street lights and phone lines in Hawaii.

Likewise, the Soviet Union conducted nuclear tests in space as part of Project K between 1961 and 1962. The tests caused electrical grid failures, disabled phone lines and triggered a fire that destroyed an entire power plant in Kazakhstan.

The trials demonstrated the immense risk that atomic explosions in space pose to civilian infrastructure and communication on Earth, prompting the superpowers to seek an agreement that would ban nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in space.
Analysts argue the treaty fails to address some of the challenges of modern times.
Jessica West, a senior researcher at Project Ploughshares, a Canadian peace and security research institute, said the legal framework governing space needed to be “fundamentally changed.”

She said that while the Outer Space Treaty acts like a “constitutional foundation” that remains relevant and applicable, the international community has not done the “hard work” to build a legal structure around the treaty, especially when it comes to improving verification mechanisms for space activities and expanding principles to banning conventional weapons in space.

Michelle Hanlon, executive director of the Center for Air and Space Law at the University of Mississippi School of Law, agreed, saying there is a “gap” in the treaty when it comes to barring conventional weapons.
International efforts to negotiate a new framework banning all weapons in space have stalled because there is no agreement on what counts as a space weapon, among other things, according to Samson.
A lot of the capabilities are “dual use,” meaning they can be used for civilian and military purposes, which makes it difficult to define what constitutes a weapon, she said.
“You can get up close to a satellite to refuel it, but you can also get up close to a satellite to release objects at it, shine a laser at it, or try to jam it,” Samson said.
The discussions on banning weapons come at a time when the U.S. under President Donald Trump has placed a growing emphasis on space.

In 2019, during his first term, Trump created the Space Force as a separate military branch. In his second term, he has announced the “Golden Dome” missile defense system, which includes plans to put weapons in space.

Attempts by Russia and China to introduce a new treaty to prevent the placement of all weapons in space have hit a wall, in part due to the lack of a definition. Additionally, Washington says it ignores ground-based anti-satellite missiles that when used create massive amounts of dangerous space debris.

In November 2021 Russia launched such a missile to destroy a defunct Soviet-era satellite, creating more than 1,500 pieces of debris that increased risk to U.S. and Russian astronauts aboard the International Space Station and China’s Tiangong space station.

With progress on the full treaty apparently stalled, international negotiations have shifted their focus to discussing responsible behavior in space, such as avoiding the accumulation of space debris.
Samson said the U.S. has had a policy of avoiding the accumulation of space debris for many years because the debris can interfere with space flight safety and harm the U.S. self interest.
She also said that for the same reason there is a possibility that the space weapons Meink referenced could be non-kinetic weapons such as jammers.

Space debris is generated not only by kinetic space weapons but also when satellites collide and get smashed into countless fragments and smaller particles that travel at high velocity and are capable of destroying or damaging more spacecraft.

“If you start having collisions causing more debris, and more debris causing more collisions, you run the risk .. of this irreversible cascading effect,” said Steven Freeland, who is emeritus professor of international law at Western Sydney University as well as professorial fellow at Bond University.
According to the European Space Agency, there are about 46,950 pieces of debris that are regularly tracked by space surveillance networks in Earth’s orbit.
Based on statistical models, the agency estimates there are millions more smaller pieces of space junk circling Earth’s orbit.
Manzuk reported from New York.

title: Trump names national intelligence director Jay Clayton to lead a new federal AI task force
summary: President Donald Trump has tapped his director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, to lead a new government task force on artificial intelligence
story: President Donald Trump has tapped his director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, to lead a new government task force on artificial intelligence
WASHINGTON -- WASHINGTON (AP) —
President Donald Trump on Sunday tapped Jay Clayton, his director of national intelligence, to lead a new government task force on artificial intelligence.

Trump is calling it the “Super Intelligence Force,” because he has tried to rebrand AI as “super intelligence.” The announcement comes after Trump hosted top executives of AI companies at the White House last week and said they had signed a voluntary accord that would effectively self-police the development of the technology.

The task force will coordinate the federal effort "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump in a post on social media Sunday.
The task force will reach out to consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers and AI companies, the Republican president said.

Others on the task force include the Federal Trade Commission's chairman, Andrew Ferguson; Emil Michael, the Pentagon’s chief technology officer; and Scott Kupor, the director of the Office of Personnel Management.
The group will report to Trump and his chief of staff, Susie Wiles.

title: A reckoning on social media addiction came late for many kids. Will AI safety be different?
summary: The lengthy campaigns to protect kids on social media offer some lessons for those looking to protect children using artificial intelligence
story: The lengthy campaigns to protect kids on social media offer some lessons for those looking to protect children using artificial intelligence

Years after the risks of social media for kids first became apparent, U.S. states this summer reached an accord hailed as a turning point for child safety. Meanwhile, a new generation of children has begun engaging with an even more potent technology: artificial intelligence.

While the efforts to make social media safer are still taking shape, they offer some lessons for those looking to protect children using AI — technology that is growing so quickly, the extent of its risks for young people and their development is just emerging.

When Meta agreed to changes to its social media platforms and enhanced safeguards in an $18 billion settlement, it made progress by “getting at what we’ve known for years” about the dangers, said Kristin Bride, a parent advocate who has fought for social media reform since the death of her teenage son. “How are we going to get at what we don’t know is coming?”

AI companies have begun rolling out some safety features introduced first by social media companies, including age assurance measures and restricted experiences for minors. But advocates say the most important takeaway from the efforts of parents, tech companies and regulators to find a way forward on social media safety may be to act sooner on mitigating AI's harms for kids.

“The greatest legacy from the social media experiment and learnings is that hopefully we’re not going to sleepwalk into this next tech revolution,” said Dr. Dana Suskind, a professor of surgery and pediatrics at the University of Chicago, and author of “Human Raised.” “We learned that we had it all backwards, right? You don’t unleash something on a population, figure out if it does harm or not in real time, and then go back and say, ‘Oops.’”

Concerns around social media have centered on the amount of time kids spend on platforms like Instagram and TikTok, and the consequences for their mental health. Advocates also have focused on data privacy and kids' vulnerability to cyberbullying or predators who find them online.

Artificial intelligence can be more pervasive for kids. Children not only see AI-generated content on social media platforms, but they can also readily communicate with AI chatbots, including some on social media apps. Many use it for help with school and homework. Some have formed unhealthy relationships with chatbots, and experts have raised questions about how access to AI is affecting children's brain development. Companies are pushing AI-powered toys for kids as young as 2.

Campaigns for social media and AI safety for kids are both playing out on legal and legislative fronts. Individuals and states have sued tech companies over concerns around their products’ safety and both state and federal lawmakers are grappling with how to regulate the tech.

Compared with social media companies, AI giants have been moving somewhat more quickly to add safeguards, motivated perhaps by the growing regulatory and societal scrutiny of social media’s effects on kids’ mental health.

OpenAI introduced teen accounts in August, about four years after launching ChatGPT, with restrictions that include a ban on romantic chats and any suggestions that the chatbot has personal feelings toward the user.
Meta, which bought Instagram in 2012, didn’t launch teen accounts on the platform until 2024.

In announcing the settlement agreement this summer, Meta said that “ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative” for the company. Meta also urged its competitors, TikTok and YouTube, to adopt some of the standards it is implementing as a result of the settlement.
The protections outlined in the Meta settlement cannot easily be applied to AI because of the differences in the way young people interact with AI versus social media, experts said.

One of the challenges of restricting AI for minors is that it’s “much easier to point to the upsides” for teens compared with social media, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of Cornell University’s Tech Policy Institute. While there are concerns about cheating, for instance, kids are also using AI for tutoring and legitimate homework help.

“It’s not a matter of just saying ‘let’s limit this to two hours’ or 'let’s limit this between the hours of 10 at night and 6 in the morning’ because there are these salutary uses of AI that I think are harder to justify in the context of social media,” Kreps said.

A majority of U.S. teens — 64% — say they have used AI chatbots, according to the Pew Research Center. Looking up information and getting help with schoolwork tops the list of uses, though 47% say they’ve used chatbots for fun and 42% have used it to summarize an article, book or video. About 12% have turned to bots for emotional support or advice.

Jonathan Haidt, a social psychologist and author of “The Anxious Generation,” said he is most worried about the relationships and attachments young people can build with chatbots and the “cognitive offloading” that happens when people defer their thought processes to a chatbot.
“I have long thought that AI is a much bigger threat to children even than social media,” Haidt said. “But if we can’t win on social media, then it will be hopeless on AI.”
While recent litigation has held social media companies responsible for harms to users, federal legislation of social media has meandered and AI legislation has lagged.

The Trump administration has said regulation, especially across states instead of at a federal level, could hinder AI companies’ growth and sacrifice American labs’ lead in the global AI race, but some lawmakers are trying to move the needle.

Some AI legislation specific to children’s safety issues — like youth privacy, chatbot interactions and AI toy safety — have passed through Senate subcommittees with bipartisan support, but there’s still a long road for any such legislation to pass. Legislation at the state level is moving faster, as seen also in the role states have played in pushing Meta on social media harms.

“One of the things we’ve seen with social media, which I think will still be true with AI, is that we live in a federal system where states make laws on everything from e-bikes to driving permits to gun laws and that federal legislation or federal rules are much more difficult,” Kreps said.
Some say the biggest win from the progress on social media safety this year has been heightened awareness of online dangers for kids.

Bride, whose son Carson died after experiencing severe cyberbullying on Snapchat, said it’s encouraging to see legislators wrestling with how to regulate AI, but acknowledged the reality that legislation can’t keep up with the technological developments — and that kids will continue to experience AI-related harms in the meantime.
“I don’t think we can afford any more mea culpas when kids are concerned,” she said.

title: Accused Cornell fraternity member pushes to remove New York AG as special prosecutor
summary: The fraternity member's attorney said James' social media post "demonstrated a bias and presumption of guilt" of his client.
story: An attorney for the student pointed to one of Letitia James' social media posts.

One of the men accused in a "gang rape" at Cornell University is pushing to have New York Attorney General Letitia James thrown off the case, arguing that she "demonstrated a bias and presumption of guilt" through a past social media post.

An attorney for student Gillio Lopes asked an Albany court to void Gov. Kathy Hochul's appointment of James as special prosecutor in the case, as well as force the appointment of a new prosecutor "who is free from actual or perceived conflicts of interest or bias."

Lopes' attorney also pushed back on the details of the accusations made by the Jane Doe, saying her story "changed significantly" over time. Doe's lawyer has in turn said those arguments are self-serving.

Hochul appointed James to investigate the case last week after saying she lost confidence in the Cornell University Police Department and the Tompkins County District Attorney, who had previously declined to bring charges in the case
The legal push to remove James from the case centers on a social media post from last month when James signaled her solidarity with Jane Doe.

"What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I'm holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you're not alone. We stand with you," James said on social media on Sept. 28 commenting on a news article about the case.
James declined to comment on the post during a press conference last week.
"I will not comment on a Facebook post," she told reporters. She has not otherwise commented.
But Hochul defended the decision to appoint her.

"I have every confidence in our attorney general to do what she has always done. Look at the facts, examine the record, and draw the proper conclusions. That's exactly what's going to happen in this case," Hochul said.
Attorney Andrew Miltenberg, who's representing Lopes, argued in the court filing that James' social media statement about Jane Doe was enough to justify voiding the appointment.

"Through this official public statement, Attorney General James has made clear that she has formed an opinion about the case, that she believes the allegations made by Jane Doe, and that she has already reached the conclusion that Petitioner and the other named Defendants are guilty," he wrote.
Thomas Giuffra, the attorney representing Jane Doe, said she was in no condition to consent.
"She was not. Think about it. They were loading her up with ketamine. They were loading her up with -- she was drunk before she walked in the door," Giuffra told ABC News.
Lopes was suspended for one year after being found responsible for participating in the sexual activity when Doe was "incapable of conveying consent," according to Miltenberg.
Lopes was also ordered to take "an educational restorative class" and submit an essay. He has since continued his education at Cornell.
In an interview with ABC News on Thursday, Miltenberg argued that James' past statement as well as the current public attention on the case makes it impossible for his client to be treated fairly.
"By saying what she said, posting what she posted several days later, you could reasonably read that as her, Letitia James, having accepted the factual premise of the allegations," he said.
In the interview with ABC News, Miltenberg pushed back on what he described as "a nonstop barrage" of misleading information about his client.

"I think that his life and the lives of the other young men has already been destroyed in the court of public opinion," said Miltenberg. "I don't know how he ever overcomes this. He has been absolutely condemned by public opinion on social media, and that's a significant issue."
Miltenberg pointed to a now-viral exchange when Lopes was accosted on Cornell's campus earlier this month.
"Are you like not embarrassed to be here?"  a woman asked Lopes in the video. "You're a disgusting person. Everyone at Cornell is ashamed of you."
The case has rocked the university and started conversations about treatment of alleged sexual assault on college campuses.
The woman at the center of the Cornell case, a former student identified only as Jane Doe, originally made a complaint to campus police in November 2024, three weeks after the incident occurred.

The Tompkins County district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, reviewed a summary of the woman's statement that same month and decided based on that information that although the conduct in the case was "morally disturbing," it did not constitute a crime.

Van Houten reopened the case on Sept. 27 after speaking with Jane Doe and her lawyer in the wake of a civil suit being filed alleging that she had been drugged and raped. The men have denied all wrongdoing.
Jane Doe has alleged that Lopes sexually assaulted her and later snorted ketamine from her body. Miltenberg denied the ketamine use and argued that the sexual activity was consensual.
Miltenberg argued that Jane Doe's account has "morphed almost dramatically" since she first told police about the incident.

"There is a lot that is in the file that didn't make its way into the civil complaint, which tells a very different story," he said. "I think that the most respectful way for me to say it is that Jane Doe's story has changed significantly since the complaint."

title: At least 35 killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine, officials say
summary: A passenger bus was struck in Kramatorsk, in the Donetsk region, officials said.
story: A passenger bus was struck in Kramatorsk, in the Donetsk region, officials said.

LONDON and LVIV, Ukraine -- At least 35 people were killed and over 30 others were injured across Ukraine in Russian attacks on the country overnight and into Thursday morning, according to Ukrainian authorities.
In a single strike on a passenger bus in Kramatorsk, in the Donetsk region, at least 30 people were killed and 18 were injured, according to a statement released by the city council on Thursday.

"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there is absolutely no military target," the city council said. "A passenger bus. A civilian vehicle. People simply going about their daily business."
Public transport in Kramatorsk has been suspended, the statement added.

The killings overnight brought the death toll from Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past 48 hours to at least 60, following a deadly Wednesday in which at least 25 people were killed in strikes across the country, including 22 in an attack on a residential building in Pryluky.
At least four of the victims in Pryluky were children, officials said.

"Even after such a brutal attack, the Russians continued striking our regions," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday. "This morning, Russia hit an ordinary public transport stop in Kramatorsk with an aerial bomb."

title: Health officials report 74 new measles cases in Pennsylvania
summary: Pennsylvania is reporting 74 new measles cases since Monday, the state's health department said Wednesday.
story: Five people have died in the state.
Pennsylvania is reporting 74 new measles cases since Monday, the state's health department said Wednesday.
A total of 1,078 cases have been reported in the state so far this year. At least 207 people have been hospitalized and five people have died, officials said.

"Of the 74 cases added, more than 40 represent individuals who were sick more than two weeks ago and are no longer contagious, but their cases were only recently reported and subsequently confirmed, the state's department of health said. Wednesday's update "does not reflect a current surge in new infections."

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective in preventing measles infection and two doses are 97% effective, the CDC says.
Infants aged 6 to 11 months living in or traveling to high-risk outbreak areas may receive an early third dose of the MMR vaccine.

However, CDC data shows vaccination rates have been lagging in recent years. During the 2025 to 2026 school year, 92.4% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, according to data. This is lower than the 95.2% seen in the 2019 to 2020 school year, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic.

In Pennsylvania, more than 8,800 doses of the MMR vaccine have been administered by DOH staff. Of those doses, about 3,500 were administered in August and more than 2,500 were administered in September.

title: Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped trying to repair campaign sign
summary: The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office said a report was filed on Aug. 31.
story: The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office said a report was filed on Aug. 31.
A Democratic congressional candidate in Arizona says she was raped over the summer while trying to repair a campaign sign.

Bernadette Greene-Placentia, who is running in the state's 8th district to try to unseat GOP Rep. Abe Hamadeh, told the Phoenix New Times, a local news outlet, that she was attacked at around 2 a.m. as she was walking toward a campaign sign in a parking lot in Sun City, north of Phoenix.
Greene-Placentia said she was attacked, subdued and then woke up to find that she was being raped by an unknown assailant.

Greene-Placentia told the news outlet she reported the assault to the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office, and that she chose to tell her story because she had been talking about fighting for Arizona residents while campaigning "and I didn't feel like I could keep saying that if I weren't also fighting for women that are victims of sexual assault."

The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office confirmed to ABC News that a report was filed on Aug. 31 and that there is an ongoing investigation, but said the office could not comment further on the investigation.
In a statement to ABC News, a campaign spokesperson said the attack happened around 2 a.m. on Aug. 14.

"Bernadette made the difficult decision to speak publicly about the assault because she wants other survivors to know they are not alone," the spokesperson said. "She is grateful for the support she has received from the community and asks that her privacy be respected as she continues to process what happened."
In a phone call with ABC News, Greene-Placentia's campaign manager, Isaiah Lopez, confirmed that she went "missing in action" for two days following the assault.

Lopez said the campaign was at a canvass event in Chandler, Arizona, a couple days after the alleged assault on a Sunday, and she was "noticeably distraught." He said he and her communications manager spoke with her privately that day while the campaign event was still going on where she told them that she'd been raped while repairing campaign signs.

In a statement, Greene-Placentia's opponent in the House race, Hamadeh, said: "I have read the disturbing story and call upon authorities to investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place in order to prosecute the crime to the fullest extent of the law. No American should become a victim of a crime in their own community."

title: Trump interrupted by protesters as he fights to rally Texas voters
summary: President Donald Trump fought to rally Texas voters behind Senate candidate Ken Paxton as a series of protests disrupted his rally in San Antonio
story: President Donald Trump fought to rally Texas voters behind Senate candidate Ken Paxton as a series of protests disrupted his rally in San Antonio

SAN ANTONIO -- President Donald Trump, facing protesters and a poor political climate, fought to rally Texas voters behind Senate candidate Ken Paxton on Wednesday night in a bid to stave off sweeping Democratic victories in the nation's most populous red state.
But Trump's remarks were not focused solely on Paxton.

Speaking to a packed Freeman Coliseum, Trump also pledged to award retired baseball star Roger Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom, restated his support for the death penalty for drug dealers and clarified recent comments in which he talked about the possibility of Iran bombing American cities as part of a recurring riff about how high fuel costs are “a small price to pay” for the war.
“You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego, let them hit Los Angeles,” Trump said. “We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities. We protect our country.”

The president's message was interrupted repeatedly by protesters, including by one who appeared to be close to the stage. In all, at least a dozen demonstrators interrupted the president. Some were led away by police.
Trump stepped away from the microphone briefly after one interruption.
“He’s going back home to mom,” Trump said. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”
The Republican Party did not plan to devote so much money and manpower to Texas this midterm season.

Texas is the nation’s most populous reliably Republican state, where Trump won in 2024 by almost 14 percentage points. But with Election Day less than a month away, Trump’s poor approval ratings, the Iran war and soaring gas prices have threatened Republicans in virtually every state.
Wednesday’s appearance marked Trump’s third trip to Texas in less than a month, and party officials have devoted more than $300 million to elections in the state so far.

In a sign of Trump’s poor standing, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott did not attend the evening rally. A three-term Republican governor who won reelection in 2022 by roughly 11 percentage points, even Abbott has been caught in the turbulent national currents.
He’s locked in a competitive reelection race against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa.
Instead of appearing with Trump, Abbott was scheduled to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on the governor’s absence.

“For years, Greg Abbott has never been shy about embracing Donald Trump, calling Trump a ‘great friend’ and championing his agenda every step of the way,” said Texas Democratic Party spokesperson Jacob Long. “But now, as Texas families get crushed by record-high prices driven by Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran, suddenly Greg Abbott has somewhere else to be.”

While the race for governor has drawn a sudden influx of cash from Democrats, the state’s U.S. Senate race has drawn the most attention as Democrats fight for the chamber’s majority. The state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, but candidate James Talarico’s fundraising, Trump’s low approval rating and nagging concerns about Paxton’s character have put the race squarely in play.
Trump spent most of his remarks focused on the Senate contest, describing Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America.”
“He was tough and he was with us all the way,” Trump said of Paxton, whom he endorsed in the state's GOP primary over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. “He’s a fantastic man.”
Trump made no mention of the recently leaked recording of Paxton lamenting the war in Iran and rising fuel prices, while also complaining his campaign was being run by operatives in Washington.
He repeatedly criticized Talarico, including on the death penalty, a point that would appeal to many conservatives in the state that leads the nation in executions.

Trump restated his support for the death penalty for “large scale drug dealers, human traffickers and anyone who kills a police officer,” while acknowledging that Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army major who killed 13 people in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad.
The president approved the method of execution earlier this week and suggested that Talarico opposes it.
The Talarico campaign did not immediately respond when asked about the candidate’s position on Hasan’s scheduled execution.
Paxton, invited onstage near the end of the rally, heaped praise on Trump, who stood behind him: “I am so grateful that you’re here."

While Trump promoted Paxton briefly at the beginning of his remarks, he spent almost as much time later talking up Clemens, the retired Red Sox and Yankees pitcher who has been denied a spot in Major League Baseball's Hall of Fame due to his alleged involvement with performance-enhancing drugs.
Trump brought him onstage and said he'd be awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, which is the highest civilian honor — and, Trump said, “a step up” from the Hall of Fame.
Clemens said he was stunned by the honor.

“This supersedes anything that obviously I’ve done in my playing career,” he said, standing alongside Trump. “And to get it from this man, this president. ... You talking about a winner? That’s a winner right there.”
Peoples reported from New York and Beaumont reported from Des Moines, Iowa. Associated Press writer Will Weissert in Washington contributed.

title: Trump announces 'historic' enrollment of 70 million children into Trump Accounts
summary: Trump hails what he called "historic" enrollment of 70 million American children into his Trump Accounts.
story: "They'll end up being quite rich by the time they're 18," Trump said.

President Donald Trump on Wednesday hailed what he called the "historic" enrollment of 70 million American children into his Trump Accounts, calling them “a step to ensure every American child has a fair shot at the American Dream.”

The administration announced that beginning on Oct. 1, the Treasury Department automatically enrolled 60 million children under age 18 in the president’s signature investment accounts in addition to the 10 million whose parents opted into the accounts following their official release on July 4.

“With automatic enrollment now complete, every American child under the age of 18 has a Trump Account in their name, making it easier than ever for families to participate,” White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.

According to the administration, $2.2 billion has been deposited into the accounts since their release on July 4. The Treasury Department pledged to pour a one-time $1,000 seed contribution for each child born between Jan. 1, 2025 and Dec. 31, 2028. Children born outside of that range will not receive the seed contribution from the Treasury — but their family members and acquaintances are able to deposit money into the accounts. Several corporations — including Uber and Nvidia — and philanthropists — such as Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell and his wife, Susan, who seeded the program with a $6.25 billion contribution, also donated to the accounts.

Trump, encircled by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett, and the Dells, predicted, "So if all goes well, which I think it will, they'll end up being quite rich by the time they're 18 and then 21."

Trump said in January when he announced the initiative that a number of major U.S. companies pledged to match the federal government's initial contribution for eligible employees' children, including Charles Schwab, Robinhood, SoFi, Uber, Charter Communication and BNY, and that several others had agreed to make contributions.

In a notice published in the Federal Register, the Treasury Department said that auto-enrollment was geared to maximize children’s participation in the accounts, estimating that an additional 2 million children would benefit from the accounts every year as a result.
“An eligible individual should not lose the opportunity to receive contributions or investment growth merely because no adult completed an election,” the Treasury wrote in the notice.
Starting Oct. 1, parents no longer have to opt-in to the accounts, but can claim their children’s accounts on the Trump Accounts app.

According to the administration, the accounts are designed to boost future financial security for the most recent generation of Americans, with each child gaining access to the account in their name once they reach the age of 18. They can then allocate the funds in the account solely for purposes designated by the Treasury Department — including paying for university tuition or purchasing a house.
Some Democrats have praise the program. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore called it a "smart policy," and California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who called it "one of the best things [Trump] has done."

Democratic Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Democratic Rep. Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts introduced a similar proposal in 2023, which would have provided each American child with $1,000 at birth in an account that they could access at age 18, but it didn't make it out of committee. Booker also supported Trump's proposal.

title: Flight attendants' union flags safety concerns over Trump's Washington arch
summary: The union representing flight attendants has raised safety concerns about President Donald Trump's proposed triumphal arch near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport
story: The union representing flight attendants has raised safety concerns about President Donald Trump's proposed triumphal arch near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport

WASHINGTON -- The union representing thousands of flight attendants said Wednesday it has safety concerns about President Donald Trump's proposed triumphal arch that will be on final approach to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.

Association of Flight Attendants-CWA President Sara Nelson said the 250-foot (76 meter) arch compounds multiple safety concerns that she said have gone unaddressed from a deadly January 2025 crash over the Potomac River that killed 67 people. Nelson also criticized Trump's plan to turn the arch into "a top grade military complex” able to host drones and snipers while storing ammunition.

“DCA is already stretched to its limit, we do not need an obstacle taking up space in our flight path,” said Nelson. “Nor should commercial aviation have to dodge military drones, missiles or snipers while attempting to take off or land at Washington National Airport. Safety first always.”

Nelson’s statement on behalf of the union, which represents 55,000 flight attendants across 20 airlines, joins the voices of an assemblage of veterans’ groups, Congress members and others with safety concerns and complaints about the memorial's threat to historic and symbolic sightlines between different landmarks in Washington, D.C.

Though the arch has received early approval from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, whose members were all tapped by Trump, a group of three veterans and an architectural historian sued, saying the project needs to be approved by Congress.

Last month, the Republican president said in a social media post that he had agreed, at the “strong request” of the military, to convert the planned 250-foot-tall (76-meter) memorial arch “into a top grade Military Complex.”

The Federal Aviation Administration said last month before Trump's announcement on it becoming a military complex that the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft, but it should be “appropriately marked with a non-standard eternal flame on top of the structure and floodlight projectors pointed towards the arch to make it noticeable for pilots.
An assessment by the National Park Service said the memorial arch could disrupt the historical significance of dozens of nearby sites. The Park Service approved the project despite its assessment.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced early last month that excavation work on the site in Memorial Circle would begin within weeks. The Interior Department did not respond immediately to questions on the status of that work.

The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.
This story has been updated to correct the union’s name. It is the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA , not Flight Attendants Association-CWA.

title: 9/11 families seek release of documents they say include Saudi's link to attack
summary: Sept. 11 victims' families made their case in a federal appeals court Wednesday, seeking release of documents they say may link Saudi Araba to the attacks.
story: Sept. 11 victims' families made their case in a federal appeals court Wednesday.

Families of Sept. 11 victims asked a federal appeals court on Wednesday to order the government to release documents they say tie the Saudi Arabian government to the plot to hijack airplanes and crash them into New York and D.C.

After 90 minutes of legal questioning over the fate of their lawsuit against the Saudi government, families of the 9/11 victims seemed hopeful that a panel of appellate judges would allow their case to move forward and to continue pursuing evidence about the Kingdom's role in the attacks.

"[The judges] were not buying what [Saudi Arabia] were selling," said Terry Strada, whose husband was killed in the attacks and who publicly called on the Trump administration last month to support their efforts. "This was a very good day for us."

The Saudis want the case thrown out, claiming they have immunity from civil litigation as a sovereign foreign government despite Congress enacting a law nearly a decade ago meant to grant victims of terrorism the opportunity to sue alleged state sponsors of terrorism.

The three-judge panel of appellate judges on Wednesday largely steered clear of the merits of the case -- whether the Saudi government supported hijackers who carried out attacks in Washington and New York -- and focused narrowly on dense jurisdictional matters.
The hearing in the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit in New York extended long past the allotted time for oral presentations.

If the judges rule in favor of the families, the case could proceed to trial as soon as next year and would open the door for the families to pursue more evidence that could cast light on the Kingdom's role in the attacks.

"Give us our trial ... we want our day in court,” Brett Eagleson, who lost his father on 9/11, said at a news conference following the hearing. "What you saw today is Saudi Arabia grasping at straws."
Both Eagleson and Strada reiterated past calls for the Trump administration to step in and "hold [the Saudi government] accountable” and to "put America first."
The judges took the matter under advisement. Lawyers involved in the case don't expect a ruling until early 2027.

With past presidents in attendance at this year’s 9/11 commemoration in New York, marking 25 years since the attacks, several family members openly faulted the U.S. government for keeping these materials secret.

"Administration after administration, including leaders in front of us here today, chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families," Strada, the widow of 9/11 victim Tom Strada, said during the ceremony.
President Trump was not present at the New York commemoration and instead attended a commemoration ceremony at the Pentagon.

"President Trump is leading the most transparent administration in history, which is why he authorized the declassification and release of hundreds of pages of documents related to the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001," the White House said in a statement released the afternoon after the 9/11 commemoration in New York.

Evidence released so far as part of a lawsuit traces the activities of Omar al Bayoumi, a Saudi national who had been living in California. The families, citing FBI records released during the Biden administration, say he was a Saudi intelligence asset who assisted at least two of the hijackers. As ABC News previously reported, the families say Bayoumi aided those two hijackers by "finding them an apartment in his complex" and "providing funds just below the suspicious activity reporting threshold to help them open a bank account,” according to the families’ lawsuit.
Many of the 9/11 hijackers were Saudi nationals, according to the FBI, along with a few others from the United Arab Emirates, Egypt and Lebanon.
The Saudis have repeatedly denied having any role in facilitating the 9/11 attacks and said in court Wednesday that they remain "an ally of the United States [and] a sworn enemy of Al Qaeda."
The decision on whether to declassify additional 9/11 records ultimately lies with President Donald Trump, whose administration has touted government transparency.

A White House spokesperson told ABC News last month that "President Trump is leading the most transparent administration in history, and his team is working diligently to identify records that are responsive to these families' request."

title: 'We hope not': Trump says US doesn't believe Russian plague is a bioweapon
summary: President Donald Trump said he has a phone call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss the issue.
story: Trump said he has a phone call scheduled with Russian President Putin.

President Donald Trump said Wednesday that the U.S. doesn’t believe the reported death of a lab worker from an anti-plague institute in Siberia is related to a bioweapon, but he acknowledged that Russia has not been forthcoming with information, saying “Russia is not saying much.”

“Well, we don't think so. We're going to find out soon enough, but we don't think so," the president told reporters in the Oval Office when asked if the plague in Russia was a bioweapon. "And they're saying it's very much under control. So, we hope not.”

Asked if he believes Russia is sharing enough information on the suspected plague case, Trump said Russian officials have shared "a little bit with our people. We expect them to share it a lot with our people," adding "We have brilliant experts. They know everything about what's going on, and all of that information is going through them."

Trump also said he has a phone call “set up” with Russian President Vladimir Putin, a claim he also made on Tuesday, which he said then would happen "probably tomorrow." The president said their conversation was expected to touch on the heightened scrutiny of Russia's response after some Russian media and public figures reported a death potentially connected to the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute.

The Kremlin has said no such phone call between the two leaders had been scheduled. In response to an ABC News request for clarification, the White House referred to the president's comments Wednesday.

The U.S. has issued a formal diplomatic complaint known as a démarche over the Russian government's response to the reported death of a lab worker from an anti-plague institute in Siberia, urging the country to increase transparency surrounding the incident, ABC News has learned.

"We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government. We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information," a State Department spokesperson said.

A U.S. official said early Wednesday that the démarche was transmitted to representatives of the Russian government within the last few hours. The démarche itself is classified, but the official said it reminds Moscow of its requirements to comply with international health regulations.

Russian authorities have said only that that the case of the lab worker’s reported death was "pneumonia of an unknown cause," with the health agency Rospotrebnadzor saying tests showed no link with her work. They issued a statement saying that "no accidents have been detected at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute while working with pathogenic microorganisms."

Rospotrebnadzor's office for the Irkutsk region issued on Tuesday a statement, saying, "A false message is being circulated online about the introduction of an enhanced sanitary and epidemiological regime and strict restrictions in the Irkutsk region."

The U.S. Embassy in Moscow said in a Tuesday health alert that it was aware of the press reports, saying, "We continue to track the situation closely." The State Department reminded Americans not to travel to Russia, saying the U.S. government has limited ability to help its citizens who go there. Additional restrictions may be in place for some regions, the embassy said.

Presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday that official information would come directly from Rospotrebnadzor, adding, "the media are reporting a great deal right now, and the overwhelming majority of what the media are reporting around this situation is false information."

Rospotrebnadzor issued an additional statement Wednesday, stating in part that "the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk Region and the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov is calm" and that "preventive and anti-epidemic measures have been organized in full, and there are no epidemic risks to the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk Region."

"In accordance with the International Health Regulations, Rospotrebnadzor sent information about the situation to the World Health Organization," the statement further said, adding "preventive and anti-epidemic measures have been organized in full, and there are no epidemic risks to the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk Region."

As Russian officials came under scrutiny, U.S. officials offered to provide assistance. Trump said the U.S. was willing to help Russia after the U.S. State Department announced it was monitoring the reportedly fatal case of "pneumonia of an unknown etiology."
"Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we're always willing to help," Trump told reporters Monday.
Asked about how the U.S. is planning to mitigate the risk coming from Russia, Trump said that his administration is "looking at it very strongly."
Russia said it would welcome help from the United States, but also sought to downplay concern.

"It is always very good when mutual assistance is offered," Peskov told journalists on Monday. Peskov then appeared to downplay Trump’s suggestion the issue was a “major problem for Russia,” telling a journalist he had not heard that framing.
"To be honest, I did not hear the president’s words that he considers this a major problem for Russia," Peskov said. "As far as I remember it was not said that way, although I may be mistaken."

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, asked Tuesday in Iceland by ABC News whether he had reason to believe there has been an accidental release of an intentionally modified strain of the plague, said it would "irresponsible for me here to sit and speculate because we just don't have all the information yet."
"I think it's incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world. That's what they should do," the secretary said.
Rubio said his department was tracking the situation "hour by hour."

title: Dems push back on Trump admin's 'brazen' attempt to roll back education standards
summary: Democrats are urging HHS Secretary Kennedy to stop proposed changes to Head Start, calling the reforms illegal and "antithetical" to the mission of Head Start.
story: They're calling on HHS Secretary Kennedy to stop proposed changes to Head Start.

Democrats are urging Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to stop the Trump administration's proposed changes to Head Start, calling the reforms to the early childcare and education program illegal and "antithetical" to the mission of Head Start.

Head Start, the largest federal childcare program, aims to ensure that more than 700,000 kids receive a high-quality pre-school education for students ages 3-5 and improve welfare outcomes for children and their families. The reforms transfer federal oversight to state programs.

In a letter led by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, a bicameral coalition of lawmakers accuse the federal health department of proposing to "gut" the program by rolling back 90% of its performance standards and it asks Kennedy to withdraw the changes outlined in the agency's recent announcement.

But the new administrative changes could diminish program quality, reduce disciplinary standards, eliminate jobs for educators and healthcare providers and weaken protections for students with disabilities and unhoused families, according to the letter that was first obtained by ABC News.

"This proposed rule is a brazen attempt to dismantle Head Start without regard for the hundreds of thousands of young children and working-class families who depend on these programs and services every year," the lawmakers wrote in the letter to Kennedy's office on Wednesday.

In addition to Sanders, who serves as the ranking member on the Senate’s Health, Education, Labor and Pensions committee, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, House Education Committee ranking member Bobby Scott and more than 150 other Democrats signed onto the letter.

The lawmakers allege that the proposed changes violate the Head Start Act -- the law that authorizes the eligibility and standards for the program -- and illegally eliminate the program's core components of giving vulnerable students and families a boost in life. For more than 60 years, the program has provided early childhood education, health, nutrition and family support services to low-income children and families.
Head Start has undergone major revisions under previous administrations, including the largest reduction in funded Head Start slots in program history.

Since FY16, Head Start enrollment has declined from over 1 million children to 771,121 in FY25, according to government data. The National Head Start Association supports the government's intent to reduce unnecessary burden on Head Start programs and educators but the organization said the proposed rule exceeds its deregulatory approach.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services contended that any Head Start program that likes its current performance standards under the federal government's previous guidance is welcome to maintain those standards.

"Head Start teachers and staff are exceptional professionals who have in many cases dedicated their lives to serving children and families," the spokesperson wrote. "It is a shame that some elected leaders in Washington do not trust Head Start directors, teachers, and parents to make wise decisions for the children they serve but instead believe Washington must tell all 1,600 Head Start centers across the U.S. exactly how they have to run their programs."

Early childhood advocates stress that new regulations requiring English-only instruction, caps on administrative spending, and shifts in health screenings could also harm future Head Start participants.

Wednesday's letter comes as the 60-day open comment period for the changes ends. Kennedy's uncle, Sargent Shriver, founded the program in 1965. The secretary has said that the reforms will remove unnecessary bureaucracy for hundreds of thousands of American families to renew the "promise of Head Start for the next generation" by allowing local Head Start centers more authority over their programs.

In their letter, the lawmakers scolded the proposal saying Kennedy "made a commitment to Congress to 'preserve' Head Start," during his confirmation hearings -- "yet this proposed rule is the latest attempt by the Administration to deteriorate and ultimately eliminate the program by gutting the core standards and services that have long-defined and ensured its success."

Meanwhile, the Trump administration's goal to make the largest revision to federal childcare policy in decades aligns with current administration priorities. If implemented, the new regulations would empower parents, implement the new federal dietary guidelines and physical activity standards, shift early childhood governing authority to the states, and eliminate duplicative layers of compliance, according to the health department. The department also awarded over $200 million to Head Start for nutrition, facilities, and other services last month.
For now, as federal funding remains intact and programs are still operating, Head Start proponents told ABC News that fewer federal regulations should not mean fewer results for its families.
Bernadine Futrell, who served as the Biden administration’s Head Start director, told ABC News that the program is life saving and provides critical services.

"It's more than early learning," Futrell told ABC News, adding "It is an early childhood program. It's focusing on brain development, health and nutrition, healthy habits, financial literacy, economic mobility for parents, and it's a two-generational approach – where it's not just a child being served; it's the entire family that is moving to another level."

title: Maine Senate debate: Collins and Jackson spar over Trump, trade and abortion
summary: Sen. Susan Collins drew on her seniority in Congress to counter Troy Jackson, who portrayed her as ineffective in pushing back against Trump’s agenda during their debate.
story: The two also debated ICE and Trump's signature tax and policy bill.

In their first debate in the closely watched race for Senate in Maine, incumbent Sen. Susan Collins drew on her seniority in Congress and her role as chair of the powerful appropriations committee to counter Democrat Troy Jackson, who portrayed her as ineffective in pushing back against President Donald Trump's agenda.

"As chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, I've been able to bring home federal dollars to help ease the burden on our taxpayers. In the past five years, I've secured $1.5 billion for 672 projects ... these are investments in our communities," Collins said during the debate Tuesday.

As Trump's trade war with Canada continues, Collins referenced her behind-the-scenes work to minimize the pain for Maine, whose economy is intertwined with Canada, including getting certain products removed from the tariff list.

"I have been the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs with Canada. Canada is not China. It is our neighbor, our friend, our closest ally, and our biggest trading partner. So, I have been strongly voting against the tariffs with Canada, but I've also been working behind the scenes," Collins said. "I was successful in getting concrete, pulp and road salt removed from the tariff list," Collins said.
Jackson, though, said what Collins has done is not enough, arguing Trump's policies are driving up the cost of goods and living and that "she won't talk back against Donald Trump,"
"I didn't mock the fact that she got road salt back. I mocked the fact that what about everything else? We can't eat road salt," Jackson said.
Jackson referenced Collins voting for Trump's signature legislation, the "One Big Beautiful Bill," out of committee, saying it's "crucifying Maine."

Collins voted against the final passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill because of the cuts to the Medicaid program, but said she voted to send it out of committee because of the billions of dollars to fund rural health care.
Jackson doubled down, though, on the fact that Collins voted the bill out of committee.

"Senator Collins is like an arsonist who helped set the fire, and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out. I mean, she advanced the bill out of committee. You just heard her say it ... If she'd have stopped it, she wouldn't be able to do the other things, meaning that she could have stopped it."
On the Iran war, Collins mentioned her past votes to end the war in Iran and how the war has led to a rise in gas and diesel prices.
"I think that it is not well thought out. It has caused adverse circumstances in terms of the cost of global oil," Collins said.
As Trump has mentioned possibly campaigning in Maine ahead of the November election, Collins was asked whether she would campaign with him, and she said she believes he won't come to the state.

"I don't think that President Trump is going to come to Maine," she replied. "He's talking about going to a lot of different states. I've heard nothing from his office, and I'm not exactly his favorite senator."

Jackson attacked Collins heavily over her vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, even referencing her vote in his opening remarks during tonight's debate, which falls on the anniversary of her vote for the justice.

"[Brett Kavanaugh] helped overturn Roe v. Wade, and today she says she has no regrets," Jackson said. "And I would, you know, wonder for everyone, including myself, would you trust her to pick the next Supreme Court of Justice?"
During the portion of the debate where the candidates could ask each other questions, Jackson asked Collins if she would admit she was wrong to vote to confirm Kavanaugh.

Collins said she does not agree with Kavanaugh's vote to overturn Roe v. Wade and referenced her support of Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson. When the moderator asked whether she felt Kavanaugh lied to her, Collins said Kavanaugh should not have asserted that Roe v. Wade was settled law.

"I do not feel that he lied, but I think that he should not have said it was settled law because, to me, that meant that it would not be overturned. But to be fair, you cannot ask a nominee how he might vote on some hypothetical future case."
Collins, who has been a long supporter of abortion rights, called out Jackson for previously being against abortion access early on in his political career.
"So, I would point out that there's only one of us on this stage who has always been pro-choice, and that's me," Collins said.
On immigration, Jackson referenced the fatal ICE shooting in Biddeford, Maine, earlier this year and called for ICE to be disbanded and for funding to be redirected to Customs and Border Protection.
Collins pushed back on abolishing ICE, but said the agency needs "serious reform."

title: Trump proposes Camp David-style presidential retreat at his private Florida golf club
summary: President Donald Trump says he wants to turn part of his private West Palm Beach golf club into a retreat for future presidents and their guests, similar to Camp David near Washington
story: President Donald Trump says he wants to turn part of his private West Palm Beach golf club into a retreat for future presidents and their guests, similar to Camp David near Washington

FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. -- President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he wants to develop one of his Florida golf courses into a presidential retreat where his successors can spend quiet weekends on the greens, describing it as “sort of a Camp David ” that he says would already have many of the security features needed to host presidents and world leaders.

The proposal for the retreat on Trump’s private golf course in West Palm Beach would comingle the presidency with Trump's business ventures beyond his time in office, and is the the latest example of Trump seeking ways to leave his imprint on the presidency.
“It’s a great idea, and it’ll be used a lot,” Trump said, claiming it was suggested by the United States Secret Service. “It seems that all presidents play golf.”

The plan has already been submitted to local officials. Trump, an avid golfer, rattled off the benefits of the property a short drive from his Mar-a-Lago home during an unrelated event in the Oval Office, noting that it’s close to an airport and has some distance from residential homes and tall buildings, which pose security risks.

He did not mention that the golf course was the site of an unsuccessful attempt on his life in 2024. Trump was playing at the Trump International Golf Club during a break from the campaign trail when a Secret Service agent spotted an armed man in the trees lining the club’s perimeter fence. The man was arrested after a chase and later convicted of trying to kill Trump, and was sentenced to life in prison.

Past presidents have used Camp David, a rustic compound in Maryland, as a weekend retreat and a place to host presidential meetings. Trump has spent less time there, often opting for his own properties, including golf clubs in Florida, New Jersey and Virginia.

Trump's proposal follows other projects by the lifelong real estate developer to build a White House ballroom, gild the Oval Office, erect a triumphal arch, renovate the Kennedy Center, refurbish the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and rebuild a golf course in East Potomac Park. He has also begun planning a future presidential library in a Miami skyscraper.

In a letter to Palm Beach County commissioners last month, first reported by the Palm Beach Post, an attorney who represents the golf course said Trump is offering to designate it as a “U.S. Presidential Golf Course.”
“Just as Camp David, Windsor Castle, or the Elysée Palace are known worldwide, so too will the Presidential Golf Course in Palm Beach County,” Harvey Oyer said in the letter.

Palm Beach County Administrator Joseph Abruzzo said in a statement that local officials are eager to explore what this “historic opportunity” could mean to the community. “This likely would further cement Palm Beach County’s place on the national and international stage for generations to come,” Abruzzo said.

Oyer's letter said the West Palm Beach golf course could be used by current and former presidents, along with visiting foreign heads of state. The Trump Organization owns the golf club but leases the land from the county, which would need to approve any changes.

Under the proposal, the club would pay to build a new presidential lodging and then work with the Secret Service and other agencies to provide free access to the federal government. The retreat would have a separate entrance from the private club, which earned Trump nearly $37 million during his first year back in office, according to his financial disclosure.

“This is a gift that the President would like to share with his successors, the people of America, and his fellow Palm Beach County residents," Oyer wrote. "It should be noted that President Trump will be out of office before this proposed project could be completed so this is a gift to his successors.”

Oyer highlighted past U.S. presidents who turned over land for public use. Dwight Eisenhower donated his Gettysburg Farm in Pennsylvania to the National Park Service, and Franklin D. Roosevelt donated part of his estate in Hyde Park, New York.
Years before it was bought by Trump, Mar-a-Lago itself was proposed as a “Winter White House.”

Businesswoman and socialite Marjorie Merriweather Post left the home to the National Park Service when she died in 1973, but the agency returned the home to her estate in 1980 because of high maintenance costs. Trump bought the property in 1985, and it later became his primary residence.
Binkley reported from Washington.

title: Canadian poet who combines classical and modern wins Nobel Prize in Literature
summary: Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson who combines the classical and the modern wins Nobel Prize in Literature
story: Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson who combines the classical and the modern wins Nobel Prize in Literature
STOCKHOLM -- Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson who combines the classical and the modern wins Nobel Prize in Literature.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.
The Nobel Prize in literature will be awarded Thursday by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm.

Last year, Hungarian writer László Krasznahorkai, whose surreal and anarchic novels combine a bleak world view with mordant humor, won the Nobel Prize in literature for work the judges said upholds the power of art in the midst of “apocalyptic terror.”

Three science awards were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award recognized a scientist’s efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The chemistry prize recognized two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.
This week ends with Friday's peace prize. The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.
Dazio reported from Berlin.

title: Hurricane Isaias is expected to get stronger on its way to Florida, Alabama and Mississippi coasts
summary: Isaias is surging toward the U.S. Gulf Coast as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season
story: Isaias is surging toward the U.S. Gulf Coast as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season
Isaias surged toward the U.S. Gulf Coast on Thursday as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, prompting mandatory evacuations and school closures in parts of Florida.
