title: Trump aide's daughter pictured with pro-Russia politician
summary: Katie Wiles is a partner at the political lobbying firm Continental Strategy. A spokesperson for the firm acknowledged to CBS News on Thursday that Wiles had taken the trip to Republika Srpska but not on business.
story: An image circulated on social media and verified by CBS News shows Katie Wiles, the daughter of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, recently traveled to Republika Srpska, the Bosnian-controlled territory led by pro-Russian Serb strongman Milorad Dodik.

The photo raises further questions about possible White House links to the pro-Russian politician. President Trump on Wednesday distanced himself from two top political advisers after the New York Times reported they had traveled to Republika Srpska last week to assist Dodik's pro-Russia party in Bosnian elections.

The image, shared online by conservative Albanian American activist Evi Kokalari, shows Wiles holding a rifle and standing next to a man CBS News has identified as Željko Budimir, the interior minister of the semi-autonomous Republika Srpska administration. In a post on X, Kokalari claimed the image was taken in August. CBS News Confirmed has verified the image is of Wiles and that it was taken in Republika Srpska. The image appears to be a screenshot of a story from Wiles' personal Instagram account, with a caption "mostly work + some serious fun!"

CBS News confirmed the veracity of the images through satellite imagery and previous social media posts from the shooting range where the image was captured. The position of the sun in the image also indicates that it was taken in the summer. CBS News was also able to confirm that the woman in the photo is Katie Wiles.
The RIS shooting range is located in northern Republika Srpska and is frequented by Budimir, the interior minister, according to Bosnian media reports.
Katie Wiles is a partner at Continental Strategy, a large political lobbying firm based in Washington, D.C., according to its website.
A spokesperson for the firm acknowledged to CBS News Thursday that Wiles had taken the trip in mid-August but not on business for Continental Strategy.

"Katie Wiles visited the country in mid-August for two days with a U.S.-based company who was invited to do a feasibility study in the region," the spokesperson said. "Wiles provides strategic communications support to this US company and has done so for over two years. Wiles has not spoken with any United States Government official regarding Srpska."
CBS News has asked Continental Strategy for the name of the company and whether the American company in question is a client of Continental Strategy.
U.S. foreign agent registration filings [FARA] reviewed by CBS News show that Continental Strategy registered to lobby on behalf of Republika Srpska in early 2026.
"Susie does not discuss work matters with her daughters," a White House official told CBS News Thursday.

Another FARA filing from the same firm this year lists the signature of Alejandro Garcia, a former deputy political director for Mr. Trump's presidential campaign, as a consultant for Republika Srpska. Garcia is also a partner at Continental Strategy.
The lobbying firm's spokesperson told CBS News that Garcia attended Bosnia's election day on Oct. 4 "but no other member of the team was present."

"Garcia is the sole person who has interacted with the United States government regarding Srpska, and his contacts have all been meticulously tracked to be reported in accordance with FARA requirements," the spokesperson said.

White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles met with Željka Cvijanović, a close ally of Milorad Dodik, last month, and a White House official told CBS News that meeting was arranged by Garcia, not by Katie Wiles.

On Tuesday, the New York Times reported that James Blair and Chris LaCivita, two key GOP strategists in the Republicans' midterm election efforts, spent some of last week in the small, self-governing territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina to help Dodik's party with its own campaigning.  Katie Wiles has no such involvement with Mr. Trump's political operation.

Under the control of Dodik's party, Republika Srpska has forged close ties with President Vladimir Putin's government in Russia, while also spending heavily on U.S.-based lobbying firms to court associates of Mr. Trump, according to FARA filings reviewed by CBS News.

Serbian secessionist leader Dodik, who until recently served as the president of Republika Srpska, has long been accused of undermining the U.S.-brokered Dayton Accords, which ended the bloody sectarian violence between Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia in the 1990s. A Sarajevo court last year convicted Dodik of failing to comply with the terms of Bosnia's 1995 peace accords. He was then removed as president and banned from holding political office by Bosnia's electoral authorities.
In a Truth Social post Wednesday, Mr. Trump said he did not "have any idea" who LaCivita and Blair had been working for and he pledged, "if there's a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!"
Later Wednesday, Mr. Trump appeared to slightly soften his language.

"They don't have a conflict, because they're independent people. You know, they don't work for me," Mr. Trump said, addressing reporters in the Oval Office. "They are consultants and I assume they have a lot of clients. I don't know who their clients are. If I thought they had a conflict here, I would terminate them."

As CBS News reported this week, the involvement of a U.S. firm linked to associates of Mr. Trump in an energy project in Bosnia and Herzegovina worth more than $1.5 billion has raised questions about the White House's relationship with Dodik.

Last month, House Democrats published a report accusing the Trump administration of lifting sanctions against Dodik in an effort to enrich and empower allies of Mr. Trump, and of undermining longstanding U.S. foreign policy interests in the region in the process.

The central allegation is that AAFS Infrastructure & Energy, a company incorporated in the U.S. last year and headed by Mr. Trump's former personal attorney Jesse Binnall and Joseph Flynn, the brother of Trump ally Gen. Michael Flynn, secured the contract to build a key gas pipeline between Bosnia and Croatia after the sanctions were lifted against Dodik, who had previously opposed the development.

FARA filings cited in the report and reviewed by CBS News show that Michael Flynn, Mr. Trump's former national security adviser, worked as a paid lobbyist for Republika Srpska in October 2025, the month during which the sanctions against Dodik were lifted.

Within six months of the sanctions being lifted, Dodik's party, which has veto power in Bosnia's legislature, dropped its opposition and the Bosnian parliament passed legislation naming AAFS as the lead developer on the billion-dollar project.
The White House declined to comment on the pipeline project last week, but an administration official said the sanctions against Dodik were lifted to prevent instability in the Balkans.

"This is yet another example of President Trump's pragmatic, farseeing foreign policy that has prevented disasters on perennial issues that his predecessors so often stumbled into," a White House official told CBS News on Friday, without elaborating on the type of disasters the Trump administration was preventing.

title: Protesters ejected from raucous Trump rally in Texas
summary: Several hecklers were removed from President Trump's rally in Texas late Wednesday, drawing jeers from the crowd as the president made fun of the protesters.
story: At least 18 hecklers were removed from President Trump's rally in Texas late Wednesday, the Bexar County Sheriff's Office confirmed.

The hecklers were ejected from the venue by authorities or appeared to walk out after interrupting the rally, drawing jeers from the crowd at San Antonio's Freeman Coliseum as Mr. Trump mocked the protesters.
The sheriff's office said they did not make any arrests, and all individuals were asked to leave the premises. Two people were issued criminal trespass warnings, the sheriff's office said.
It's the president's third trip to Texas in recent weeks to support Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, who is facing a tougher-than-expected contest against Democratic candidate James Talarico.

Less than 10 minutes into Mr. Trump's speech, a person stormed away from the stage while yelling. At one point, a man in a red hat grabbed that person's hair and appeared to get into a physical altercation, leading other rallygoers to separate the two. After the person walked out of the venue, the president asked: "Is there anything like a Trump rally?"
"He's going back home to mom right now," the president said. "What he doesn't know is that his mom voted for Trump."

For the next hour, several other people were walked out of the venue by law enforcement or security while the crowd booed them. In some cases, Trump supporters and demonstrators were separated after physically tangling with each other.
At least one person was handcuffed before law enforcement led him out.
The president poked fun at several of the attendees who were ejected, saying one person has "got to lose a lot of weight" and others were "really bad-looking people."
CBS News has reached out to local authorities and the U.S. Secret Service for more information on the ejections.

Mr. Trump was on stage for well over an hour. He spent much of the event railing against Talarico, a state lawmaker who is aiming to be the first Democrat to win a statewide race in Texas in more than three decades. Most polls show Talarico either with a narrow edge or neck-and-neck with Paxton, a state attorney general with a polarizing record who frustrated other Republicans by ousting Sen. John Cornyn in a primary earlier this year.

Republicans have sought to cast Talarico as too liberal for Texas, a theme that Mr. Trump emphasized throughout the evening, jabbing Talarico for his record in the state legislature. The president said if Talarico wins, he would turn Texas into a "dirty, failing, crime-ridden third-world dumping ground."

Mr. Trump also spent a large amount of time on immigration, touting the precipitous drop in unauthorized border crossings in recent years. The issue dominated Mr. Trump's 2024 campaign but has become more challenging for him as most voters grow skeptical of his administration's hardline enforcement tactics — particularly Hispanic voters, whose shift toward Mr. Trump helped propel him to victory in 2024.

title: Mamdani criticized for statement mourning Oct. 7 and condemning Israel
summary: A statement by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani that recognized three years since Hamas' "horrific" attack on Israel — and criticized Israel's "ongoing genocide" in Gaza — has drawn fury from some Democrats.
story: A statement by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani that recognized three years since Hamas' "horrific" attack on Israel — and extensively criticized Israel's "ongoing genocide" in the Gaza Strip — has drawn fury from some Democrats.

Mamdani is a longstanding and vehement critic of Israel's actions during its war with Hamas in Gaza, and an opponent of U.S. aid to Israel — issues that have divided Democrats nationwide and drawn criticism for the mayor from moderates, leaders of Jewish groups and Israeli officials. Mamdani has long defended his stance, saying criticism of Israel is distinct from antisemitism.

Wednesday's statement by Mamdani began by calling it a "profoundly painful" day for many New Yorkers, noting Hamas' "horrific war crimes" on Oct. 7, 2023, including the killing of about 1,200 people in Israel and the taking of more than 250 hostages. He added: "We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss."

The mayor then shifted to criticizing Israel for its "devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza" — noting the more than 74,000 deaths recorded in the enclave, according to the Hamas-controlled Gaza Health Ministry.
"Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them — all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes," Mamdani said.

"Three years later, we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment," Mamdani added.
Several Democratic elected officials blasted Mamdani's statement, arguing it was too focused on Israel rather than Hamas.

Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz of Florida accused Mamdani of "desecrating the memory of murdered, innocent Jews," Rep. Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey said the mayor was "blam[ing] the victims" of the Oct. 7 attack, and Jersey City Mayor Steven Fulop called the statement "inappropriate and unnecessarily inflammatory."

Rep. Richie Torres, a Democrat who represents the Bronx, penned an X post that did not name Mamdani, but said: "Perhaps, for just one day—October 7th—the critics of Israel could take a vacation from their hysterical hatred of the world's only Jewish State and find it within themselves to express condolences for the thousands of Israelis murdered, maimed, mutilated, raped, and abducted at the hands of Hamas."
Rep. Daniel Goldman — who lost a Democratic primary in his Manhattan and Brooklyn district to Mamdani-endorsed Brad Lander earlier this year — called the mayor's message "reprehensible."

"In the guise of 'grieving' with those mourning that day, Mayor Mamdani asserts as fact hotly disputed allegations that he knows full well will offend and further upset those same people he pretends to grieve with," Goldman wrote on X.
Lander, the Democratic nominee in Goldman's deep-blue district, wrote a statement of his own on Tuesday that condemned Hamas but argued against the "flattening of empathy."
"We can mourn for those lost on October 7th and still acknowledge the enormous imbalance of power between Israel and the Palestinians," Lander wrote in a post on Substack.

Mamdani also faced pushback from the Anti-Defamation League, whose CEO, Jonathan Greenblatt, is a frequent critic of the mayor. Greenblatt wrote on social media that in Mamdani's statement, "not once do you say 'Jews.'"
"You are weaponizing a day meant for mourning the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust to recycle your usual antizionist talking points," Greenblatt wrote.

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee called Mamdani's statement an "outrageous & disgusting rant," while Ofir Akunis, Israeli consul general in New York, called it a "disgrace, shame, and insult to the memory of those who were murdered."
CBS News has reached out to Mamdani's office.
Mamdani's stance on Israel has drawn intense scrutiny — and applause from his allies — since he began his unexpected ascent to the mayor's office.

Ahead of the 2025 Democratic mayoral primary, Mamdani vowed that if Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited New York City, he would seek Netanyahu's arrest on an International Criminal Court warrant accusing him of war crimes.

Over the summer, Mamdani conceded that the city did not have the power to execute the warrant. The U.S. is not a party to the global treaty that created the ICC and generally does not recognize its authority. Israel has called the war crimes allegations "absurd and false."
When Netanyahu visited the city last month to address the United Nations General Assembly, he accused Mamdani of antisemitism and said "many Jews no longer feel safe in New York."
"Shame on you for distorting the facts, shame on you for inverting victim and aggressor, shame on you for spitting in the face of truth," Netanyahu said.
Mamdani has long rejected allegations that his strong criticisms of Israel have fueled antisemitism, and says the city "has no room for hate or bigotry of any kind."
Last month, Mamdani unveiled a plan to combat antisemitism, including a dedicated antisemitism hotline and funding to upgrade security at synagogues.

Asked by CBS News New York about the criticism he has faced and whether he believes he should dial back his statements, Mamdani said last month: "I think criticism of a prime minister, criticism of government policy is distinct from bigotry of a people. … And what my job is to ensure is not only that we are proud of being the most Jewish city in the United States of America, but that we also make this a city where Jewish life can continue to flourish."

title: FDA says its abortion pill safety review will continue into next year
summary: The FDA says its ongoing safety review​ of the nation's main abortion pill​ will continue into next year, a timeline quickly condemned by abortion rights foes hoping to see the drug's use curtailed.
story: Washington — The Food and Drug Administration says its ongoing safety review of the nation's main abortion pill will continue into next year, a timeline that was quickly condemned by abortion rights opponents hoping to see the drug's use curtailed.

The FDA gave a court-ordered update on its progress in a legal filing late Wednesday, providing the first substantive information about the controversial reevaluation ordered by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Mifepristone was first approved by the FDA in 2000. The agency has repeatedly reaffirmed the pill's safety and effectiveness over the years, in addition to easing a number of restrictions on the drug, including dropping a requirement that it be dispensed in person.

But since President Trump returned to the White House, anti-abortion rights groups and their allies in Congress have pushed the administration to revisit the pill, in the hopes of restricting its use.

The FDA said in its filing that it expects to complete a safety study of the pill by mid-December this year. A report on the findings is expected "no later than March 2027," after which the agency will decide whether to impose new restrictions or other changes on the drug's use.
Gavin Oxley, of Americans United for Life, an anti-abortion group, criticized the move as a lack of "true leadership" by Trump administration officials.
"The administration continues to find itself on the wrong side of women's health, clearly uninterested in mitigating the ongoing harms caused by the abortion pill," Oxley said.
The two-drug regimen of mifepristone, combined with a second drug, misoprostol, is the most common form of abortion in the U.S.

The FDA was directed to provide the latest update by a federal judge in a case brought by the state of Louisiana alleging that mail delivery of mifepristone undermines the state's abortion ban. It's one of several state lawsuits related to mifepristone winding their way through the courts.

Last month, a three-judge panel for the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals questioned the merits of Louisiana's case, including whether the state had the legal standing to challenge the FDA's oversight of mifepristone.
Any ruling from the 5th Circuit on the Louisiana case wouldn't immediately change the landscape because the Supreme Court has blocked changes to the drug until it sees the case again.

The FDA said Wednesday it is using a "statistical data mining method" to discover "unknown safety concerns" that may exist with the drug. The data comes from an electronic database that collects reports of medical injuries and drug side effects from major health networks and insurers.
In addition to the safety study, the agency said it is considering a number of petitions proposing changes to how mifepristone is prescribed and distributed.

Abortion opponents have focused most of their efforts on a 2021 decision allowing doctors to prescribe the drug online and send it through the mail during COVID-19. That decision, made permanent under President Joe Biden in 2023, had the effect of undermining a number of state abortion bans, since women can receive the drug through the mail.

Asked in 2025 whether a review of mifepristone could lead to a ban, CBS News medical correspondent Dr. Celine Gounder suggested it would be difficult for the FDA to withdraw approval, an extraordinary step that would quickly draw legal challenges.

However, Gounder said that depending on what the safety review finds, it could make access more difficult, limiting the drug's availability through telehealth or by mail, or restricting the ability to prescribe it to doctors rather than physician assistants or nurses who are also currently able to prescribe it.

title: Stephen Miller spoke at FBI training on domestic terrorism, sources say
summary: Stephen Miller spoke at a training session at FBI headquarters just days before prosecutors criminally charged a man with making disturbing calls and texts to his wife, sources told CBS News.
story: White House homeland security adviser Stephen Miller spoke at a training conference for counterterrorism agents at FBI headquarters just over a week ago, days before prosecutors criminally charged a man with making disturbing calls and texts to his wife, Katie, multiple sources told CBS News.

Former Justice Department officials called the visit unusual, given the historical norm of insulating federal criminal investigations from political officials. The administration and FBI have said Miller's visit was appropriate, pointing to his role at the White House and the administration's broader focus on cracking down on political violence.

Miller told the agents that President Trump's initiative to counter domestic terrorism was personal to him, citing the 2025 assassination of his friend, conservative Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk, according to a source who was briefed on the meeting and a senior FBI official.

In his comments, Miller spoke about the need for federal law enforcement agents to be more proactive in investigating threat cases and told them that no case is too small, whether the threats are directed toward a congressman, a spouse, friends, loved ones or a speaker at a college campus, the senior FBI official said.

The FBI official said that Miller's remarks reflect a broader push by federal law enforcement to try to get out ahead of mass-casualty events by stepping up investigations into cases involving threats and harassment because those crimes can be precursors to violence.

The training on Tuesday of last week was attended by FBI assistant special agents in charge who specialize in counterterrorism, as well as officials from other law enforcement agencies, including IRS Criminal Investigation, Homeland Security Investigations and the U.S. Secret Service, multiple sources added.

A White House official said that Miller's presence at the training was appropriate, given his role as homeland security adviser. In that capacity, he is tasked with carrying out Mr. Trump's executive order on countering domestic terrorism and political violence.

"As Homeland Security Advisor, Stephen Miller interacts with all law-enforcement agencies on a regular basis related to public safety, national security, and counterterrorism," a White House spokesperson told CBS News.
She added that Miller is tasked with carrying out the president's executive order to "investigate, disrupt, and dismantle all stages of organized political violence and domestic terrorism."
An FBI spokesperson called the executive order "a critical directive for this FBI's work to combat domestic terrorism and political violence threats all across the country."
"Stephen Miller has been a valued partner in this work – and the conference was thrilled to have him be a part of discussing the important priority," the spokesperson said.

But multiple former Justice Department officials told CBS News that his participation at an FBI training conference is not customary, and runs afoul of the post-Watergate norms that historically insulated the Justice Department's criminal investigations from political interference by the White House.
His appearance at the event is also unusual because he is an alleged victim and potential witness in the Boston-area case involving the man accused of cyber-stalking Katie Miller, they said.

That role is further complicated by the fact that Miller and his wife have repeatedly asked the FBI's Washington Field Office to investigate political activists and others they allege have threatened or harassed them. In an unrelated case last year, Stephen Miller asked the bureau to allow agents to go undercover in his Virginia neighborhood's political activist group, several sources with knowledge of the matter told CBS News.

"Politically well-connected people who are related to victims do not have a right to jawbone FBI supervisors to do what they want them to do, and if they are political and throwing around their political connections, it's even worse," said Jeffrey Breinholt, a longtime former counterterrorism prosecutor at the Justice Department who frequently provided training to FBI agents.

In the days leading up to Miller's appearance as a guest speaker at the terrorism training session, the two most senior counterterrorism agents in the FBI's Washington Field Office were transferred to other roles by its leader, Darren Cox, after the Miller family complained the agents were not moving swiftly enough on an investigation into a man in Massachusetts who was allegedly sending taunting texts and voicemails, sources told CBS News.
Their removal was first reported by Bloomberg Law.

Two days after Stephen Miller made his presentation, the U.S. Attorney's Office in Boston charged John A. Proia with one count of cyberstalking Katie Miller and her family. Proia has pleaded not guilty.
White House officials have said that the Millers did not speak directly to the agents who were reassigned, nor did they ask for the personnel change.
A White House spokesperson said that senior FBI leadership determined the agents were "stifling investigations into very serious threats and made a unilateral decision to remove them."

In a statement provided by the FBI, Cox said: "This was a personnel decision made at the Washington field office level alone based on our constant evaluation of mission needs. Any suggestion otherwise is false."
Chris Raia, the deputy director at the FBI, said in a statement that the personnel decision was based on "a number of factors" that have not been reflected in the media's reporting on the incident.

Asked about investigations related to the Millers, an FBI spokesperson said the bureau "pursued these cases based on appropriate predicate and evidence of alleged crimes — not because the White House ordered an investigation."
The Boston case is at least the second one that the Millers pressed the FBI to bring related to alleged acts of harassment or alleged threats.

Last fall, Stephen and Katie Miller asked Virginia state officials and the FBI to investigate local Arlington political activist Barbara Wien after she protested outside their home and distributed flyers containing their address, prompting the Millers to move into military housing.

The federal case hit roadblocks after a magistrate judge twice rejected a search warrant, CBS News previously reported. But Miller repeatedly pressured the Justice Department to act, asking FBI counterterrorism agents to go undercover and regularly calling the U.S. Attorney's Office in the Eastern District of Virginia for updates, sources with knowledge said.

As recently as December, FBI agents were interviewing Wien's neighbors and acquaintances, despite not being able to obtain a warrant to search her phone. CBS News could not determine the status of the investigation, which remained open as recently as this summer, one of the sources said.

The state prosecutor who was investigating the case, Arlington and Falls Church Commonwealth Attorney Parisa Dehghani-Tafti, formally declined to bring charges earlier this year, writing in a court filing that "nothing in the proceeds of the search warrant supports criminal prosecution."
Her office is the same one that is prosecuting Colin DeMarco, who was arrested earlier this year on state charges of attempting to murder Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought.
Her office brought the case after federal prosecutors in the Eastern District of Virginia declined to bring federal charges, sources told CBS News.
The training at FBI headquarters was centered on an executive order issued by the White House last fall known as "National Security Presidential Memorandum-7."

That order called on the FBI-led Joint Terrorism Task Force to coordinate a national strategy for combating domestic terrorism and political violence. It also tasked the attorney general with prioritizing such cases.

While there is no formal domestic terrorism statute, the Justice Department has historically used a variety of other criminal laws to charge violent extremists and pursued terrorism enhancements at sentencing.
Some types of charges, such as providing material support to terrorists or civil disorder, require consultation or approval by the National Security Division.

In December, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi issued a memo to prosecutors and law enforcement that broadened the scope of the kinds of crimes that might be pursued as domestic terrorism cases, such as doxxing members of law enforcement or parading with the intent to obstruct the administration of justice.

The memo also made it clear that law enforcement should focus on people with "extreme viewpoints on immigration, radical gender ideology, and anti-American sentiment" who are willing to commit acts of violence.

The cyberstalking law that Proia is charged with violating — 18 USC 2261A(2)(B) — is not considered a statute that is associated with terrorism-related offenses or that requires any sign-off from the Justice Department's National Security Division before a case can be brought.
However, it has been used in the past in connection with some national security cases involving harassment targeting public officials.
Although the executive order was sparked by Kirk's killing, numerous law enforcement officials have told CBS News that there is a heightened threat environment more generally.
In addition to the multiple assassination attempts targeting Mr. Trump in recent years, numerous senior government officials continue to receive credible and pervasive threats.

Both Vought and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have 24/7 security details due to the frequent and credible threats they receive, sources with direct knowledge told CBS News.
Bondi, meanwhile, still maintains a 12-agent detail seven days a week despite having left the Justice Department months ago, a source with direct knowledge said.
The largest percentage of the threats directed toward her relate to the Justice Department's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein case, the source added.

A senior FBI official stressed that the bureau is not only focused on threats cases involving Trump administration officials, but also cases targeting others as well, such as a recent arrest in San Antonio of a man who is accused of threatening the Texas State Capitol because of anger he felt toward the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.

Although the White House suggested that Miller's speech at the FBI training was not unusual because of his homeland security position, his interactions with the FBI and Justice Department extend beyond issues of counterterrorism.

Last year, after Mr. Trump announced a violent crime crackdown in Washington, D.C. and ordered the National Guard and federal law enforcement to patrol the streets, Miller and White House Deputy Homeland Security Advisor Tony Salisbury both appeared at an FBI command post together.
A similar violent crime crackdown was later expanded to Memphis as well.

Since both initiatives took effect, Miller has been holding monthly meetings with the heads of the Justice Department's law enforcement components and special agents in charge in those cities — including the FBI, the U.S. Marshals Service, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, sources with direct knowledge say.
Miller is also in touch multiple times a week with the Deputy Attorney General's office to discuss fraud and immigration cases, according to sources with direct knowledge of the matter.

In a lawsuit filed last year by former top FBI officials who alleged they were unlawfully terminated, they claim that Stephen Miller was pressuring the Deputy Attorney General's office to take "symmetrical action at the FBI as had been happening at DOJ" by firing, re-assigning or removing staff who worked on matters that displeased Mr. Trump.

Multiple former Justice Department and FBI officials told CBS News they could not recall any other time in history where a White House official has had such frequent and direct contact with agents and prosecutors at the Justice Department the way Miller has.

One former official who has worked in senior positions at both the White House and Justice Department told CBS News that there was so much concern about the appearance of compromising the bureau's independence that in-depth discussions took place before a president visited FBI headquarters.

In addition to a few rare instances where presidents have directly addressed the FBI staff, such as President George W. Bush's address to thank them for their work on the 9/11 investigation, the only other examples people could recall included when President Barack Obama used the basketball court at the FBI's headquarters and when Bush went biking at Quantico.

"Stephen Miller's presence at FBI headquarters, including his speech, is a violation of an important norm," said James Davidson, a former FBI agent who now serves as president of the nonprofit FBI Integrity Project.

"The White House should have little official contact with FBI executive management and virtually no contact with FBI middle management regarding official matters or investigations — especially one in which he and his wife are victims."

title: CNN, MS NOW, Politico due back in court to fight White House ban
summary: Lawyers for CNN, MS NOW and Politico will be back in court as the legal battle continues over President Trump's decision to ban their reporters from the White House.
story: Washington — The Justice Department and lawyers for CNN, MS NOW and Politico will be back in court Thursday as the legal battle continues over President Trump's decision to ban reporters from the three news outlets from the White House over what he said is their negative coverage of his administration.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly is considering whether to grant the news outlets longer-term relief after issuing an order last month that temporarily blocked Mr. Trump's bans and required the White House to reinstate the reporters' access to the complex.
Kelly's temporary restraining order is set to expire Thursday.

Lawyers for the trio of news organizations are now urging Kelly to impose a preliminary injunction preventing the White House from depriving the news outlets and their reporters of White House access while the case proceeds.

"Every day, critically important news is breaking at the White House, and the ban will substantially interfere with Plaintiffs' ability to cover it," they argued in a filing. "The ban also inflicts an injury on all news media organizations — which now risk a similar fate if they engage in fact-based, independent reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable."

In his temporary order, Kelly said the news outlets were likely to succeed in arguing they were denied due process, since their journalists were not given prior notice that their reporting could lead to their White House access being rescinded or the opportunity to respond before they were banned. The judge said articles from CNN, MS NOW and Politico cited by the White House as justification for losing access were "routine" and, in some cases, written months ago.

The journalists regained access to the White House complex and had their press credentials returned nearly 12 hours after Kelly, appointed by Mr. Trump, issued his order. But the White House has refused to allow CNN and Politico in the Oval Office and aboard Air Force One, places that are opened up to the press pool, a rotating group of journalists that covers the president's movements each day.
CBS News and CNN are both part of Skydance, the parent company formed following the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery that was finalized this week.

Mr. Trump announced his ban in a post on Truth Social last month and said his decision was based on their "constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!" The president warned that "other Fake News Media Outlets" could also be stripped of their access to the White House.
The morning after he announced the ban, reporters from each of the three outlets who arrived at the White House for work were turned away and had their passes confiscated by the Secret Service.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed their joint lawsuit on Sept. 21 and asked for a temporary order blocking enforcement of the president's ban.

The following day, the White House sent letters to each of the three news outlets informing them that certain articles they had published on topics including the new White House ballroom, the ongoing war with Iran and the Republican midterm convention were threats to national security and violated standards of "professionalism and decorum" for reporters.

Most of the articles identified by the White House, which it said "threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods," were authored by reporters who do not have White House press credentials. Additionally, one piece from Politico, published in June, was based on a press call organized by the White House. During that call, the White House instructed reporters to attribute quotes to a "senior administration official," according to court papers.
The White House gave CNN, MS NOW and Politico a Sept. 25 deadline to respond to the letters, but the Justice Department said each declined to do so.

In urging the judge to continue blocking Mr. Trump's ban, lawyers for CNN, MS NOW and Politico said it "blatantly" denies them due process. The administration's "professionalism" standards and purported national security concerns are too vague under two appeals court decisions to ensure adequate notice, they said.

"At base, the empty, malleable supposed standards cited by the White House do nothing but authorize Defendants to punish reporting they dislike in violation of the Due Process Clause and First Amendment," Ted Boutrous, who is representing the news outlets, said in a filing.

Boutrous also argued CNN, MS NOW and Politico are entitled to relief on First Amendment grounds. The ban unconstitutionally retaliates against the three outlets for newsgathering and speech, and was based on the president's dislike of their "negative" coverage of him and his administration, he said.

The plaintiffs noted that the Trump administration has continued to retaliate against them even after Kelly's temporary order, demonstrating that the White House's "motive is to punish and chill journalism they dislike."

Since announcing the ban, the White House has "sought to justify the President's 'ban on the free press' with a series of shifting rationales, lurching from unarticulated standards of professionalism to nebulous and pretextual concerns about protecting national security," Boutrous said in a filing. "But all the while, the President himself has continued telling anyone who will listen precisely what this ban is really about."

The Justice Department has defended Mr. Trump's ban and said it is allowed under the First Amendment because he has two compelling reasons for denying CNN, MS NOW and Politico White House access: enforcing minimum standards of professionalism for journalists and safeguarding national security information.

"At a bare minimum, it is a significant violation of decorum to publish classified and sensitive national security information," Michael Velchik, senior counsel of the Justice Department's Civil Division, wrote in a filing.

The Justice Department also argued that the news outlets are unlikely to prevail on their due-process argument because the White House provided them "adequate notice" that their journalists' conduct could lead to the ban and the opportunity to respond. In the letters, the president informed the reporters "about the principles of decorum expected and required" of reporters who cover the White House, Velchik  said.
"After all, access to the White House is a privilege — not a right," he wrote.
Mr. Trump has continued to denounce the news outlets targeted by the ban, telling reporters that he only wants "real news, not fake news" organizations covering him.
When asked by Time magazine last week about the impetus for the ban, the president said, "it's just bad story after bad story."
"I don't think anybody should be forced to bear fake news, constantly bad stories, because I've done great things," Mr. Trump said.

title: Fears about kids' online safety unite Democrats and Republicans
summary: Amid a decline in youth mental health, momentum is building for a federal crackdown on social media companies over protections for kids.
story: The U.S. Senate candidates in Texas could hardly be more different: James Talarico, a former seminarian turned Democratic state lawmaker who speaks in calm cadences about love and empathy, and Ken Paxton, the pugnacious Republican state attorney general who speaks about a refusal to compromise.

They share an enemy, though. They dislike social media's effects on children's mental health. Talarico, who did not respond to a request for comment, has endorsed a social media ban for kids under 16, while denouncing "predatory algorithms that divide us on an hourly, daily basis." As a legislator, he co-authored a bill targeting explicit deepfakes — digital imitations of individuals that are often made or manipulated by artificial intelligence and used for harassment on social media.

Paxton has been suing Big Tech, alleging the companies hook youth on their apps or don't restrict sensitive videos from being viewed by kids. "When elected to the U.S. Senate, he will continue his proven record of advancing policies that protect children online, strengthen parental rights, and hold Big Tech accountable when it breaks the law," Paxton campaign spokesperson Madison Cercy said in a statement to KFF Health News.

Youth mental health is in decline. Even as researchers explore what's causing the problem, momentum is gathering among policymakers from both parties to crack down on social media companies. Several major companies are being sued, investigated, and, soon, potentially regulated. That they may be harming kids' mental health is a key reason.

Companies are starting to feel the bite. In late August, the social media conglomerate Meta reached a $17 billion settlement with a coalition of 48 states, the District of Columbia, and three territories and promised to change its policies and settings to protect children. Meta immediately took out advertisements in major newspapers, pressuring its competitors to adopt similar guardrails. Children's health advocates want to go further, with federal legislation.

Indeed, at least 35 nominees for the U.S. Senate this year have sponsored bills to curb social media, initiated investigations, or publicly lambasted Big Tech firms that, in their telling, have exploited teens and kids.

"We're protecting our children, not those profiting off their online presence," Juliana Stratton, the Democratic lieutenant governor and Senate candidate in Illinois, posted in June, trumpeting state legislation.

Congress is edging closer to passing the Kids Online Safety Act, the vanguard social media regulation bill. The bill would require social media companies to implement various safeguards, such as limiting users' ability to communicate with minors. One attempt to pass a version of the bill earned 91 yes votes in the Senate. Donald Trump Jr., the president's son, tweeted in December 2024 that the bill needed to be passed "ASAP."

Amid the momentum toward new federal regulations, Big Tech companies are lobbying for their preferred policy. Apple supports the bill, a spokesperson told KFF Health News, while Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, has spent $10 million on television advertising touting its teen accounts.

"Any youth safety legislation must put parents in the driver's seat — blanket social media bans do not do that," said Meta spokesperson Ed Patterson, who argued blanket bans push youths onto less safe platforms. "We support legislation that empowers parents — not the government — to approve the apps their teens can download from the App Store."

Meta and other industry groups are scrambling to shape regulations for social media, and tech in general. The Wall Street Journal reported Meta also gave some $10 million to a President Trump-aligned campaign nonprofit, Securing American Greatness. Based on a KFF Health News search of the Senate's lobbying database, about 70 corporations, trade groups, nonprofits, and other groups have been lobbying senators about the bill.

According to The Washington Post, the Trump administration has tried to tie the online safety bill to other parts of its AI agenda, which includes legislation that would make it harder to regulate the technology at the state level. The White House did not respond to requests for comment.

The public's views of major tech firms are souring. In 2024, the Pew Research Center found 78% of Americans said tech companies had too much influence in politics, while 64% said social media had a mostly negative effect on the country.

A widespread movement encompassing much of the public health establishment, parents' groups, attorneys general, and whistleblowers is calling for greater regulation, as parts of the tech industry fight back by spending big on lobbying and marketing.

"You have the whole industry and all their lobbying dollars," said Allison Ivie, chief policy officer at the Eating Disorders Coalition. Many experts believe that social media, by showing kids images of unrealistically thin peers and by amplifying content encouraging extreme diets, helps fuel eating disorders. "It's not a balanced fight by any means," Ivie said of the lobbying muscle. "How do you compete against that on any given day?"
Growing up online, breaking down offline

According to 2025 data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, a third of youth have persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness — about 10% more than a decade earlier. But many researchers question whether social media is causing the trouble. (Other metrics tracked by the agency show improvement.)

"The science is crude and messy," said Sandro Galea, dean of public health at Washington University in St. Louis, who previously chaired a National Academy of Sciences report on the effects of social media on kids' mental health. Academics and researchers have proposed a wide variety of causes for the crisis, like changes in the economy, decreasing social connections, access to firearms, and the pandemic.

Despite the uncertainty, much of the public health establishment is massing against social media. In early September, the Department of Health and Human Services hosted a three-hour event advising parents and children to live life off-screen. It's only the latest in a series of warnings from the U.S. surgeon general's office — under both the Biden and Trump administrations — about these technologies.

"The evidence keeps building on the real and potential dangers of unregulated access for children," Jerome Adams, Mr. Trump's first surgeon general, told KFF Health News. These include, he said, "serious risks like higher rates of anxiety, depression, sleep problems, and developmental concerns. Kids spending too much time on these platforms face real challenges during key stages of growth."

The policy backlash against social media has extended worldwide. The United Kingdom and Australia recently banned social media for kids under 16. The European Union has threatened Meta with a potential fine, up to 6% of revenue, for pushing "addictive designs" in a breach of the confederation's regulations.

Besides the $17 billion settlement with Meta, other lawsuits in the United States have targeted Snapchat, owned by Snap, and TikTok, a short-video app owned by a consortium of American and Chinese companies. A school district in Kentucky won a $27 million settlement from social media companies; 1,000 more districts, including in Los Angeles, have filed their own class-action suits, citing alleged addictive effects on youth, among other harms.

Coalitions of state attorneys general, including Paxton, have sued Big Tech companies, in some cases winning settlements related to allegations of mental health harm and addiction. In early August, Meta was ordered to pay nearly $950 million after a New Mexico state court found it to be a "significant contributing factor to the current mental health crisis." This preceded the multibillion-dollar settlement.

And a broad base of companies are feeling effects from the government and civil suits. The online gaming company Roblox disclosed paying $91 million in legal settlements, including expenses for "youth-related consumer protection and digital safety matters," in the first half of 2026. YouTube, the video hosting website, itself settled multiple youth-related cases this year.
Taking Big Tech to task
Yet the push in Congress has garnered much of the attention. Congressional committees on occasion have summoned tech company executives — sometimes with a friendly ear, but more often to berate them.

Accompanying the push for legislation are ongoing investigations, many of which collect testimony from whistleblowers. In 2025, Sarah Wynn-Williams — a former United Nations diplomat who later joined Meta — testified before the Senate about the company's record.

Asked about allegations the company covered up or denied its knowledge of harms, she said: "Facebook was targeting 13- to 17-year-olds. It could identify when they were feeling worthless or helpless or like a failure, and they would take that information and share it with advertisers."
For example, Wynn-Williams told lawmakers, "if a 13-year-old girl would delete a selfie, that's a really good time to try and sell her a beauty product."

Meta has been dogged by claims it has attempted to hide relevant internal research, including from the government. In a series of rulings in 2025 and 2026, a judge in Washington, D.C., found the company's lawyers directed employees to "remove portions of research showing Meta's knowledge of teen users' developmental vulnerability because the research could be used by government enforcers investigating Meta." But Meta says it has approved three dozen studies on social issues related to young people, and that they have "made real changes to protect teens online," like creating teen accounts, whose settings parents can control.

Complicating any regulatory push, though, are protections for speech and privacy. For the legislation to work, said Jenna Leventoff, senior policy counsel with the American Civil Liberties Union, "the platforms are going to want to know who is a kid and who isn't." Simply asking users will not be enough, she said. "I know when I was a kid, I always said I was older than I was to try to create accounts."
But the momentum for constraints continues. Over time, Ivie said, "we get all this damning evidence. It shifts perspectives."

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

title: Rubio calls for "unapologetic pursuit of national power" in Acropolis speech
summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio stood before the Acropolis to argue that the answer to the West's current problems can be found, at least in part, in ancient Greece.
story: Athens — As the United States wages a costly war with Iran and Europe struggles with the grinding conflict in Ukraine, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stood before the Acropolis on Wednesday and reached back more than two millennia to argue that the answer to the West's current problems can be found, at least in part, in ancient Greece.

In a speech timed to the sunset from the Pnyx, where Athenians gathered for their democratic assembly, Rubio cast ancient Greece as the source not only of Western democracy and philosophy, but of what he described as the character that fueled the West's rise.

"Here, in Athens, we found the first full realization of all the essential traits that would come to define the West," Rubio said, citing "fierce individuality and relentless ambition," and "a yearning for discovery, for adventure, risk and glory."
He argued that those modern Western societies had allowed those qualities to erode.

"The ideal of many ideologies in our time has, frankly, become a world of perfect safety, a world devoid of risk or failure, where neither the glory of victory, nor the shame of defeat," Rubio said. "We hold the most exceptional things among us hostage to the average, the ordinary, the mediocre."

His remarks were delivered before roughly 250 invited guests, including senior Greek government officials, members of the diplomatic corps and representatives of the business, educational and cultural sectors, according to a senior State Department official.

The speech expanded on themes Rubio laid out at the Munich Security Conference in February, when he warned that Europe faced "civilizational erasure" and argued that the U.S. and Europe needed to recover a shared Western identity. Still, his conciliatory tone in Munich came as a relief to European officials after Vice President JD Vance had used the same stage a year earlier to sharply rebuke the continent's leaders.

In front of the Acropolis, Rubio traced the development of the West from ancient Greece through Rome, European Christianity and eventually the United States, citing Alexander the Great, Caesar, Charlemagne and Columbus along the way. He portrayed America's frontier expansion, industrial development and space program as later expressions of the same drive.
Rubio said the West now stands at a crossroads, "because the next decade and the decisions we make will write the story of the next century."

"The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all," he said.

"Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice," Rubio continued. "We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power, to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialize our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future."

The history Rubio presented was arguably selective. He spoke relatively little about democracy or political equality at a site closely associated with both, focusing instead on competition, national loyalty and the willingness to take risks. He argued that modern societies too often seek "perfect safety" and concern themselves more with "the comfort of the worst than the potential of the best."
"The men who made the Parthenon, they built upwards. They held that the highest and most noble aspiration in life was to surpass all others, to strive to be the best in all things," he said.

The highly produced speech came during a trip largely devoted to more immediate questions of American power: where U.S. forces can operate, how NATO allies can help counter Russia and Iran, and how American energy can displace Russian supplies in Europe.

Greece was the second stop on a three-country tour that began in Iceland and ends in Portugal on Thursday. In Iceland, amid growing U.S. attention to Arctic security, Rubio left open the possibility of an increased American military presence, saying, "We'd never do anything without cooperating with officials here about what's available. I think there is a willingness to do more together."

In Athens, Rubio met Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis for the sixth U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue, focused on defense, energy and regional security. At a news conference Wednesday, Rubio called Greece a "strong and model NATO ally," while Gerapetritis said Greece could provide maritime assistance in the Strait of Hormuz if a viable peace process is established.

Rubio was also asked by CBS News whether he was confident U.S. Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle's tenure had complied with State Department ethics rules, amid congressional scrutiny over allegations that Guilfoyle used her diplomatic position to benefit private business interests in Greece.

"This is not the format where we're going to address this," Rubio said. "Suffice it to say our embassy has been doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador." Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing.
Rubio's visit and Acropolis address come at a complex moment for the Trump administration.

The U.S. is seven months into its war with Iran and has yet to secure an agreement to end it. Vice President JD Vance said this week that Iran would need to make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity, raising questions about whether the administration was backing away from its earlier insistence on zero enrichment.
Asked Wednesday by CBS News to clarify the U.S. position, Rubio declined to say what level of enrichment, if any, Washington might accept.

"I don't understand what the confusion is about the nuclear program. Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. Simple, period and end of story," he said. "I'm not going to go into, you know, into the details about what would be acceptable or not."
The war has also helped push oil and gasoline prices sharply higher, adding an economic and political cost at home as the midterm elections approach.

In his remarks before the Acropolis, Rubio directly raised Iran. After invoking the Spartans at Thermopylae and Achilles' pursuit of glory at Troy, he contrasted Western ideas of sacrifice with what he called a "cult of death" among Iran's "radical mullahs."
"Our heroes may be willing to die for their cause, but they do not worship death," he said.

The speech also comes as Rubio's own political future attracts increasing attention. President Trump has publicly raised both Rubio and Vice President Vance as possible future standard-bearers for his movement.
Rubio did not overtly mention his own ambitions Wednesday, but pointed to recent administration achievements, including the Greenland deal he helped broker last month.
"It is a vision we saw in action," Rubio said, arguing the agreement would "reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of NATO."
"We want to win together," he said. "We must win together."
Rubio later headed to Portugal for the last leg of a four-day European trip.

title: Democrats invest more heavily in Gina Hinojosa as Pritzker offers support
summary: Last week, more than 70 Latino Democratic leaders sent a letter to Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, the chair of the DGA, urging the group to invest $10 million to help Hinojosa's campaign.
story: National Democrats are stepping up their financial support for Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa after recent polls showed a dead heat and more Democrats began to see an opportunity to potentially defeat three-term incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.

Illinois Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker, a possible 2028 presidential contender, and the Democratic Governors Association are each putting at least $1 million behind Hinojosa, according to sources familiar with the investments and a senior DGA official. Pritzker's contribution is actually larger — $1.2 million, according to sources familiar with the commitment. The New York Times first reported the investment.

The infusion comes at a crucial point for Hinojosa's campaign. She reported roughly $4 million in cash on hand at the end of last month, according to campaign finance filings, and her campaign said it had been outspent by Abbott by roughly 10-to-1.
In a statement, Hinojosa's campaign said her campaign has "momentum," and said "we're grateful for the support we've received in this final stretch from leaders across the country."

Last week, more than 70 Latino Democratic leaders sent a letter to Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, the chair of the DGA, urging the group to invest $10 million to help Hinojosa's campaign. A source told CBS News on Wednesday that the state's Latino leaders, including Texas congressional lawmakers, met with the DGA to increase pressure to fund Hinojosa's campaign, which was first reported by NBC News.
A source familiar with the investments tells CBS News that the DGA took action to support Hinojosa after Pritzker committed his own money to the race.

A DGA official disputed that characterization, saying that Beshear told Hinojosa in a conversation on Tuesday of last week that the DGA would spend at least $1 million on her campaign. A source close to Hinojosa's campaign confirmed the conversation between Beshear and Hinojosa took place, as well as the Kentucky governor's $1 million  commitment.
Abbott's campaign said in a statement that she is "taking her campaign to out-of-state Democrat strongholds."

Abbott has significantly outraised Hinojosa, including from July to September, when his campaign said it brought in $20 million to her campaign's $13 million. But his campaign reported having $17 million cash on hand, indicating a huge amount of spending given the over $100 million on hand he reported at the beginning of the year.

A Democrat has not been elected to the governor's mansion in Texas since Ann Richards in 1990, who lost reelection to George W. Bush four years later, and President Trump won the state by more than 13 points in 2024. Abbott had not been considered vulnerable, but recent polls had shown the race tightening.
Mr. Trump is campaigning in San Antonio on Wednesday with Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and several other GOP candidates, although Abbott is not joining the rally.

title: Obama hosts fundraiser with Senate Democrats weeks before midterms
summary: Former President Barack Obama headlined a fundraiser for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Wednesday night to discuss the stakes of the upcoming midterm election.
story: Washington – Former President Barack Obama headlined a fundraiser for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Wednesday night to discuss the stakes of the upcoming midterm election.
The event featured a conversation between Obama and Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, vice chair of the DSCC, about Democrats' efforts to flip the Senate.

"I think he is just such a voice for our country, and of both realism and practical optimism, and I think we need that right now," Blunt Rochester told CBS News. "And I think he also lays the foundation for the significance of this election."

Senate Democrats have become increasingly optimistic about their prospects this fall after several races shifted toward the party in recent weeks, including in deep-red states like Texas and Ohio that are considered toss-ups, according to CBS News' battleground tracker.

"We do not want to be overconfident, but what we're seeing in state after state after state is that people are sick of Trump, they're sick of the Republican Senate going along with them, and they see the clear divisions we have drawn between what we stand for and what they stand for," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told CBS News last month. "That has put us on the edge of victory."
Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate. Democrats would need to pick up four seats to gain control of the upper chamber.
Meanwhile, Republicans have argued they still have a path to hold on to the Senate.

"Right now, there's a lot of noise, there always is in the political atmosphere — some of it's created by our opponents," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a South Dakota Republican, told reporters before the body went on recess. "But if we can stay focused, talk about the future and the two paths over the course of the next several weeks, based on our record of accomplishment, things we got done, things we still need to do, we've got a great argument."

One key target for both parties is Michigan. Democrats are trying to hold the seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Gary Peters while Republicans see it as a prime pickup opportunity. An exclusive CBS Detroit poll, conducted by Mitchell Research and Communications, shows Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed with a narrow advantage over GOP challenger and former Rep. Mike Rogers.

Obama is expected to campaign with El-Sayed and other Democratic candidates in the Wolverine State later this month. A source familiar with the former president's thinking said his strategy this fall is "driven by where he can move the needle with Democrats and persuadable voters."

The former president has also taped two dozen ads for Senate and gubernatorial candidates around the country. Last month, he participated in the second of two fundraisers with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, where he pressed Democrats to do more on the issue of artificial intelligence.

"Certainly if I were running for president next year, this would be one of my central agendas, and I would have a very clear plan, and I would talk about this, and I would say, 'Here's our plan for safety, here's our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this,'" Obama said. "I would be thinking about the economic impacts in very concrete ways and understanding: What does it mean if there's going to be job displacement? Where is that going to hit? How are we going to respond?"

Jeffries told CBS News he has remained in contact with Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris and expects both to be engaged through Election Day. The minority leader, who is poised to become the first Black House speaker if Democrats win control of the lower chamber, predicted that House Democrats would "take back the majority" this fall.
"It's an all-hands-on-deck effort," Jeffries said.

title: Newly obtained footage shows Iran attack on major U.S. post in Kuwait
summary: CBS News obtained new video from a person on the ground showing an Iranian attack on a U.S. base at the beginning of the war.
story: Washington — New videos obtained exclusively by CBS News show Iranian attacks on a major U.S. military base in Kuwait as the war with Iran kicked off seven months ago. American forces faced ballistic missiles, drones and what witnesses described as Iranian F-5 fighter jets.

The footage obtained by CBS News was recorded by a person stationed on the ground at Camp Buehring, and captures the moments of impact and their explosive aftermath. Damage to buildings and military equipment can also be seen in the videos.

The attacks on Camp Buehring offer a window into the strain Iranian attacks placed on American forces during the opening days of the war. CBS News has learned that soldiers defending the base ran critically low on .50-caliber ammunition as some soldiers were repositioned into the Udari Desert in Kuwait. Two soldiers were injured by lightning there in late April, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the matter.
Contacted by CBS News, U.S. Central Command, the primary unit which oversees American military operations across the Middle East, declined to comment.
The Pentagon did not comment, but pointed back to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's comments on March 4 regarding the removal of U.S. troops from bases and the employment of defensive measures.

"As we built up offensive combat power, we moved the vast majority of American troops — over 90% of Americans that were on our bases — what we say off the X, out of the range of Iranian fire," Hegseth told reporters in March.
Camp Buehring, or CBKU, sits about 25 miles from the Iraqi border and has for more than two decades served as a major staging ground for American forces deploying across the Middle East.
CBS News authenticated the videos using metadata embedded in the files and compared the footage to other photographs showing damage to the base.

Ahead of the war, sources said most of the roughly 7,000 troops there were moved elsewhere — as were the majority of U.S. forces in Kuwait — as a part of the Pentagon's "get off the X" plan, military shorthand for moving away from a position vulnerable to attack.

Once the war started, Iranian attacks, some originating from Iraq, repeatedly threatened the installation. Missiles and drones forced soldiers into bunkers. Three U.S. service members told CBS News that Iranian F-5 fighter jets were also used during the attacks, a detail first reported in April by NBC News.
"They ran so close to us I could see their helmets," the eyewitness described. "They came in, they hit us, and then took off."

While most of the U.S. service members were moved off of Camp Buehring, a tranche of more than 100 soldiers stayed behind. The service members feared the isolated base was ill-equipped to handle a mass-casualty event if the attacks continued.

"They hit us bad," the source told CBS News on condition of anonymity because of the military's strict media restrictions. "It was horrible. There were a lot of brave guys who stayed to fight there — and people at home don't know what happened. We had to abandon the base."

A senior Army official working in logistics, managing operations from another post in Kuwait, confirmed to CBS News there were concerns about the availability of .50 caliber ammunition and other "exquisite" munitions like Patriot missile batteries.

The decision ultimately was to leave. Service members packed up, loading their vehicles with whatever equipment they could and drove at night deep into the Kuwaiti desert. Their remote locations would emerge as forward operating bases, or "FOBs," where the soldiers would remain indefinitely.

No one was killed by enemy fire at Camp Buehring or at the FOBs, but several were injured, including two soldiers who were struck by lightning in desert sandstorms. One soldier suffered burns after the direct strike while the other suffered a ruptured eardrum, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the matter.

Before the lightning strike, Army leaders had been trying to move the troops out of the area, but were not able to do so quickly enough. In May, the soldiers left the FOBs for Camp Arifjan, and then relocated to other positions both in and out of the Middle East.
"CBKU got demolished," the source added. "They need to do an investigation. How come no one came to reinforce us?"

The Defense Department's inspector general last month released a report on the war with Iran that revealed "equipment losses" worth up to $3.7 billion — including nearly 60 aircraft. On Monday, the Congressional Research Service, which provides nonpartisan analysis to members of Congress, reported that 81 fixed or rotary-wing aircraft including drone assets had been lost or damaged by Iran since February, according to news reports and statements from the Defense Department.

In a first-of-its-kind mandatory report to Congress, the inspector general added that U.S. Central Command had reported Iranian strikes at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.

Although strikes were mentioned in the report, pictures and videos of any impact zones have been extremely limited. Beyond Camp Buehring, CBS News earlier obtained exclusive photos of damage at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait.
CBS News has also reported extensively on the deadliest attack of the war against U.S. troops at the Port of Shuaiba, which killed six American service members.

title: Maduro expected to face new charges of torture of Americans in Venezuelan prisons
summary: An attorney for Maduro told CBS News that he has not been given notice that additional charges could be coming.
story: Federal prosecutors are expected to bring new charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, for allegedly torturing Americans who were held in Venezuelan prisons, according to multiple sources familiar with the case.

The sources said that additional people could be charged in their role for the torture of more than a dozen Americans who were wrongfully detained by the Venezuelan government while Maduro was in power.
One source said the new charges could be announced as soon as Thursday.
Barry Pollack, an attorney for Maduro, told CBS News that he has not been provided any notice that additional charges could be coming.
Flores is due in federal court on Thursday in the Southern District of New York for a bond hearing, and a trial date has been tentatively set for June 2027.
CNN was first to report the potential new charges.
A Justice Department spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Maduro and Flores were indicted by a federal grand jury in January on charges stemming from what prosecutors said was his role in a scheme to import "thousands of tons" of cocaine into the United States and enrich themselves, their family and senior members of the Venezuelan government. The U.S. military took the couple into custody in an overnight operation and brought them to the U.S. to face the charges. They have pleaded not guilty.
Prosecutors said Maduro was at the "forefront of the corruption" and that he and his associates worked with drug traffickers and narco-terrorists to flood the U.S. with drugs.

Maduro faces four charges: narco-terrorism conspiracy; cocaine importation conspiracy; possession of machine guns and destructive devices; and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.
The case against them was brought in the Southern District of New York, where Maduro and 14 others were first indicted in March 2020, during the first Trump administration.

Maduro and his wife have asked U.S. District Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein to dismiss the drug trafficking indictment against them on the grounds that they have immunity as the leaders of a foreign country. The judge has not heard arguments on those motions yet.

In September, Alex Saab, a former minister of industry in Maduro's government, pleaded guilty to one count of money laundering tied to an alleged bribery conspiracy and agreed to cooperate in ongoing federal investigations into the regime after being deported to the U.S. from Venezuela.
In May, CBS News reported that federal prosecutors in Miami were ordered to open a new criminal investigation into Maduro amid some concerns that the pending prosecution against him is weak.
