title: An AI-generated influencer entered Alabama 'RushTok'; some fans didn't care that she was fake
summary: Olivia Moore spent $100 to create a fake RushTok influencer using ChatGPT and MiniMax, and thousands of Bama Rush fans couldn't tell the difference.
story: Olivia Moore, an investment partner at Andreessen Horowitz, used AI to create a fake Alabama
"OK, hi everyone. I’m Janie," says a curly-haired, bespectacled redhead, clasping her hands in front of her as she shyly addresses a camera from her dorm room.

"It’s day one of rush at the University of Alabama," Janie continues. Then, she mentions where she got each item of clothing she’s wearing: a pleated skirt from Abercrombie, a knit top from J. Crew, socks from Target and sneakers from Nike.

It’s Janie B's first video on her TikTok account, @jani.b086, and it’s a hit. The video, posted Aug. 8, has since amassed over 120,000 views. Its comment section is full of users doting over the college freshman. The word "adorable" is used by at least a dozen commenters.

Janie’s "outfit of the day" video, known online as an "OOTD," is a popular video format for the thousands of potential new members (PNMs) who document their experience going through the recruitment process for college sororities in an annual TikTok phenomenon known as "RushTok."
PARENTS DROP EYE-POPPING FEES ON SORORITY RUSH COACHES TO GET KIDS INTO ELITE COLLEGE GREEK LIFE

New Alpha Gamma Delta sorority sisters at the University of Alabama run to their sorority house after opening their bids inside Bryant-Denny Stadium in Tuscaloosa, Ala., Aug. 15, 2026. (USA Today Network via Reuters Co)

But Janie isn’t like the other RushTok girls who vlogged their Bama Rush experience this year. She doesn’t go to the University of Alabama. She didn’t rush a sorority. She didn’t even get her top from J. Crew or her sneakers from Nike.
That's because Janie isn’t real.
Every detail of every video on Janie’s account, from her dorm room, to her outfits, to Janie herself, was generated by artificial intelligence.

Olivia Moore, an investment partner at venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, created Janie as an experiment to understand how consumers react to AI-generated content. For only $100 in credits, Moore produced a week's worth of videos of her fake RushTok influencer participating in Bama Rush and observed as her audience argued whether Janie was real or not.
The experiment showed how quickly some viewers could detect AI-generated content and how willing some were to continue watching even after they knew Janie wasn't real.
Designing the Janie B. experiment

Moore is on the consumer investing team at Andreessen Horowitz, where she invests in companies building consumer AI products. She says she has been fascinated by "how people make and interpret and understand AI content."
"The image, video, audio models are getting very human-like very fast. I think we probably cross the uncanny valley in the next six months," Moore said in an interview with Fox News Digital.

"And, so, it means that how we as humans are able to detect AI-generated or AI-assisted content and how we interact with it is just going to become even more important because we're going to have a flood of this content, and it's going to be, in many cases, indistinguishable across all of our channels."
Moore said she created Janie as an experiment to see how consumers react to AI.

"Philosophically, that's an interesting question for me. What do people feel about AI content? What do they feel when they don't know it's AI? What do they feel when something they liked, or loved, or hated or were interested in turned out to be AI?"
CALIFORNIA LAW PUTS DIGITAL FINGERPRINTS ON AI FAKES
Recruitment prep has become its own industry, with coaches, social media strategists and designer wardrobes. (AP Photo/Brynn Anderson)

Moore primarily used ChatGPT and MiniMax to breathe life into her fake influencer. She pulled a real video of a University of Alabama dorm room off of the internet and uploaded it to ChatGPT. Then, she prompted Janie to have frizzy red hair, a pair of glasses and style from the 1960s. ChatGPT produced a still image of Janie in the real dorm room photo, and the "RushTok" influencer was born — or generated, at least.

For each TikTok, Moore animated Janie by feeding the still dorm room image into AI video model MiniMax H3. She used ChatGPT to produce prompts to feed into MiniMax, shaping how Janie would move, what she would sound like and the scripts she would follow.

Moore chose RushTok to introduce her AI influencer to the world after watching the annual phenomenon for the past five years. She said it was "the perfect testing ground" for her experiment for several reasons. Janie wouldn't be selling anything or hurting anyone, and RushTok naturally draws high traffic and has a low barrier to entry for new creators. With other PNMs participating in the trend, audiences would experience Janie alongside real humans posting similar content.
Could TikTok tell Janie was AI-generated?
On the first day of Alabama Rush, Moore introduced Janie to the world with an OOTD video. Reactions to Janie were split in the comments.

"I would say anyone under maybe 25 immediately clocked her as AI," Moore said. "But anyone in the older demographic, which is much of the Bama Rush audience, was, I would say, fooled by her and just wishing her luck and sending her good thoughts in the process."

By the second day of the experiment, the audience was mostly onto her. Moore said people took to Reddit to discuss Janie, created commentary videos on TikTok and corrected anyone who thought Janie was real in her comment section.

"By day two, day three, the comments were filled with still some people who were saying really nice things. And people would comment and tell them, 'Hey, this is AI.' And they'd be like, 'I don't care. She seems so sweet. Like, I want her to succeed.'"

As the audience caught on, Moore said she had to change her strategy. She realized that people were still willing to watch AI-generated content as long as it was entertaining enough. So, she started dropping hints in the videos and watched as digital sleuths would proudly point out clues in her comment section.
CNN, NBC, CBS INTERVIEWING VIRAL AI 'ACTRESS' TILLY NORWOOD RAISES EYEBROWS AMONG CRITICS

New Alpha Omicron Pi sorority sisters at the University of Alabama run to their sorority house after opening their bids inside Bryant-Denny Stadium in Tuscaloosa, Ala., Aug. 15, 2026. (USA Today Network via Reuters Co)
Moore said that humans are getting better at detecting AI quicker than AI generation is improving.

"We're kind of in a graph with two competing lines of different slopes. So, one of them is like, how fast is AI approaching true human-like quality? And that has gotten a lot better over the past year. The other line is how fast are humans getting better at detecting AI?" Moore said.
"It seems like, at least for now, that latter curve is higher slope. It's inflecting faster. The average human can still tell an AI video from a truly human video."
While humans could generally detect the AI content, Moore claimed TikTok, for the most part, did not immediately detect AI in most of the videos.

For the experiment, Moore decided not to label her videos as AI when she uploaded them. Of the 20 AI-generated videos she uploaded, Moore said TikTok only initially flagged 8 as containing AI-generated media. As of the date of this publication, TikTok displays an AI-generated media warning on 16 of the 20 AI videos.

"The platforms themselves are going to have a hard time detecting this content at scale, especially when the models are changing and the strategies are changing, and people are always gonna find ways to make this undetectable," Moore said.
What does the Janie B. experiment mean for the future of AI media?
Moore ended her experiment with a video of herself explaining to the audience who she was and why she decided to create Janie. She was shocked by the positive comments she received on the post.

"I think consumer sentiment towards AI is still quite negative. But if people feel like they aren't being tricked, they're being let in on it, they are being told how to do this themselves, they're being entertained by the content that's created, that can completely flip, and the feelings can be very, very positive," Moore told Fox News Digital.

Moore predicts that more consumers will start using AI tools to create human-passing content, but she says it will have to compete with human content to gain emotional investment and be as interesting and entertaining to viewers.

"I understand why people are fearful of AI because, so far, if they see AI content, it's usually something that's kind of trying to trick them versus something that is honest with them and shows them how they could get the same value," Moore said.

"The more that we are kind of honest and straightforward as people using AI around how we use it and how much of us as humans still goes into that, it'll hopefully lead to a world where AI is just another tool that allows humans to do things that are even more human."

title: Android malware can steal your PIN and bank logins
summary: RatHat Android malware uses AI to steal banking credentials, intercept two-factor authentication codes and reconstruct your PIN from touch inputs.
story: Kurt Knutsson, the CyberGuy, details an ‘unprecedented cyber incident’ in which an OpenAI experimental AI model escaped during a security test and autonomously hacked a rival AI startup. Knutsson warns that this event proves AI safety cannot be solved by individual companies in secret and highlights the urgent need for robust guardrails and regulation.

Your Android phone probably holds far more sensitive information than you realize. Banking apps, passwords and security codes can all pass through that little screen in your hand. A newly uncovered Android threat called RatHat wants access to all of it.

Security researchers at Zimperium discovered the malware, which uses generative AI as part of its attack, and found that it can turn permissions you approve into surprisingly deep control of your phone. RatHat can steal banking credentials, intercept authentication codes and even reconstruct a PIN or unlock pattern from where your finger touches the screen. It can also create a persistent connection that may survive after you remove the malicious app.

The attack still needs help from the person holding the phone. RatHat relies heavily on tricking someone into installing a malicious Android app and approving powerful permissions. That gives you several opportunities to stop it before the malware takes over.
AI MALWARE CAN REWRITE ITSELF TO EVADE DETECTION
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover five ways AI can help you get better healthcare.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare With AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
RatHat abuses powerful Android settings such as accessibility permissions and wireless debugging to gain deeper control of an infected phone. (Brent Lewin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
How RatHat Android malware gets onto your phone

RatHat starts with social engineering. Zimperium says attackers primarily spread it through SMS phishing, malicious advertising and deceptive third-party download sites. The malicious APK may pose as familiar software, including a streaming app or Chrome.

That familiar name can lower your guard. A download page might look convincing enough to make you think you are installing a normal app. However, RatHat relies on you manually installing an APK outside Google Play. Once installed, the malicious app pushes you to enable Android's Accessibility service.

The excuse can vary by region. In some cases, the malware claims the permission will solve a network problem or unlock a financial benefit. Accessibility services perform important legitimate functions on Android. However, they can also give an approved app the ability to inspect what appears on your screen and interact with the interface. RatHat takes advantage of that power to begin changing settings without you doing the work yourself.
How RatHat uses AI to gain deeper access

Once RatHat gets Accessibility access, it can tap through Android settings to enable Developer Options and Wireless Debugging. It can then read the six-digit ADB pairing code displayed on the phone and connect to the device's own Android Debug Bridge. No separate computer has to complete the connection. ADB, short for Android Debug Bridge, gives developers powerful tools to test and manage Android devices.

RatHat abuses that legitimate feature to establish shell-level access outside the normal Android app sandbox. From there, the malware launches a Go-based agent that can execute system commands. It also starts a reverse-proxy client that creates a persistent connection back to the attacker. Zimperium says that connection can give an operator continued access to the phone's ADB service. RatHat also brings AI into the process.

The malware sends information from Android's live Accessibility tree to a generative AI assistant. The AI can help determine where an item appears on the screen, read displayed text and tell the malware when to scroll. That makes the attack more adaptable than automation that follows the same fixed sequence every time. We recently saw another Android threat abuse Wireless Debugging in a similar way. RatHat adds AI-assisted navigation and another persistence mechanism to the mix.
RatHat can steal bank logins and security codes

After gaining access, RatHat can watch for financial apps and display fake screens over legitimate ones. Those overlays can trick you into entering banking credentials directly into a page controlled by the attacker. Zimperium found RatHat targeting banking and cryptocurrency apps.

It also specifically identified overlays aimed at payment services such as WeChat and Alipay. The malware can intercept SMS messages and notification content as well, giving attackers another way to capture one-time passwords and two-factor authentication codes. Then there is the way RatHat watches your fingers. The malware can monitor raw touch coordinates and compare those locations with known keypad layouts. That allows it to reconstruct PINs from where you tap.

It can use a similar method to recover Android pattern-lock sequences. Because the malware reads those touch coordinates at a low level, protections that normally hide PIN digits from screen readers do not stop this technique. That means a criminal may never need to see your PIN displayed as text. Your finger movements can give it away.
RatHat can fight attempts to remove it

RatHat also tries to make leaving your phone much harder than getting onto it. Zimperium found that the malware can interfere when you try to uninstall the malicious app. It can cancel the real uninstall process and place a fake Google Play error message on top of the screen. Even if you successfully remove the visible app, another problem remains. RatHat launches a separate native service outside the normal app life cycle.

That service can stay behind after the original app disappears. It can then reinstall the malware and restore its permissions. Zimperium also found that RatHat can request Device Admin rights. Those rights give it additional control, including the ability to wipe the device if someone tries to uninstall it. That persistence is why deleting a suspicious app may not be enough once RatHat fully compromises a phone.
What Google says about RatHat

Google responded to CyberGuy and says it has not found RatHat on Google Play based on its current detection. The company also says Android users already have protection against known versions of the malware through Google Play Protect.

"Based on our current detection, no apps containing this malware are found on Google Play. Android users are automatically protected against known versions of this malware by Google Play Protect, which is on by default on Android devices with Google Play Services," a Google spokesperson told CyberGuy.

That is reassuring for people who download their apps through Google Play. It also reinforces why keeping Play Protect enabled can add an important layer of defense if a harmful app reaches your phone from another source.
How to protect your Android phone from RatHat

RatHat becomes dangerous after it gains several layers of access. Fortunately, you can break that chain at several points. These steps can reduce your risk and help you respond if something has already gone wrong.
HACKERS HIJACK VERIFIED STREAMING ACCOUNT TO SPREAD MALWARE, RESEARCHERS FIND
RatHat can disguise malicious Android apps as familiar software, making it especially important to install apps through the official Google Play Store. (Firdous Nazir/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Avoid installing APK files that arrive through text messages, online ads or unfamiliar websites. RatHat relies heavily on persuading people to sideload malicious apps. If a page looks like Google Play, but you can see a browser address bar, you are still on a website. Close it and open the actual Google Play Store app. Also question any message that tells you to reinstall Chrome or another app already on your phone. Open Google Play yourself and check the app there instead.
2) Be extremely careful with Accessibility permissions

Accessibility access plays a central role in RatHat's attack. Therefore, treat an unexpected request for that permission as a serious warning. Open Settings and search for Accessibility. Review apps with Accessibility access and remove permission from anything you do not recognize or no longer use. Menu names can vary by Android phone. If a streaming app, browser update or other unrelated app suddenly tells you that Accessibility access is required, do not approve it until you know exactly why.

Most Android users never need Wireless Debugging. RatHat uses it to establish its powerful ADB shell connection. Open Settings and search for Developer options or Wireless debugging. Leave Wireless Debugging turned off unless you have a specific reason to use it. If you discover Developer Options or Wireless Debugging enabled and you do not remember turning them on, take a closer look at the apps and security settings on your phone.

Install strong antivirus software and keep real-time protection enabled. Security software can help detect malicious apps and suspicious activity before they get deeper access to your phone. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

However, detecting RatHat and completely removing it are two different things. Because the malware can leave behind a persistent service after the visible app is removed, we recommend a factory reset if a security scan confirms RatHat has fully infected your phone.

Google says Android users are automatically protected against known versions of RatHat through Google Play Protect, which comes turned on by default on Android devices with Google Play Services. You can still check that it is enabled. Open the Google Play Store > tap your profile picture > Play Protect > Settings. Make sure Scan apps with Play Protect is turned on. You can also enable Improve harmful app detection. This gives Google additional information about unfamiliar apps installed outside Google Play so they can be checked for harmful behavior.

Android's Advanced Protection can provide another useful barrier on supported devices. Google says it blocks app installations from unknown sources and restricts Accessibility services to verified accessibility tools. It also prevents Play Protect from being turned off while Device protection is active. To turn it on, open Settings > Security & privacy > Advanced Protection > turn on Device protection. Google notes that your phone may need to restart. For someone who rarely sideloads apps, those extra restrictions can remove two of the avenues RatHat relies on.
THOUSANDS OF HACKED SITES TRICK YOU INTO INSTALLING MALWARE
Once inside, RatHat can target financial apps and steal sensitive information, including bank logins, PINs and authentication codes. (Nicky Lloyd via Getty Images)

Install Android security updates and app updates when they become available. Updates fix known vulnerabilities and strengthen protections across your phone. RatHat's documented infection chain depends primarily on malicious downloads and permission abuse, so an Android update alone will not solve the problem. Even so, running current software closes other security gaps that attackers could try to exploit.

RatHat spreads partly through smishing, which is phishing delivered by text message. An urgent message can push you toward a malicious download before you stop to question it. Avoid tapping links in unexpected texts that tell you to install an app or fix a problem on your phone. Instead, open the company's official app or visit its known website yourself. The same advice applies to online ads offering apps. Malvertising can lead to convincing download pages that have nothing to do with the company they appear to represent.

If antivirus software flags RatHat or you have strong reason to think your phone has been compromised, stop entering passwords and financial information on it. Use another trusted device to change important passwords. Start with your primary email account since access to email can help an attacker reset other accounts. Then check your bank and credit card accounts for activity you do not recognize. If you spot anything suspicious, contact the financial institution using the number on the back of your card or through its official app.

If RatHat is confirmed, we recommend a factory reset rather than relying on a normal uninstall. RatHat's separate background component can survive after the visible malicious app disappears. Before resetting the phone, preserve personal photos or documents you know are safe. After the reset, install apps again through Google Play. Avoid reinstalling unfamiliar APK files from an old backup. You should also change credentials from another trusted device before returning to sensitive accounts on the reset phone.

RatHat can target banking credentials and authentication codes, so cleaning the phone should not be the end of your response. Continue reviewing bank statements and login alerts. Also watch for password reset messages or authentication requests you did not initiate. If you believe personal information beyond your login credentials may have been exposed, consider an identity theft protection service that can help monitor for suspicious activity. Acting quickly can limit the damage if stolen information gets used later.

The AI component makes RatHat unusual, but the attack still begins with something very familiar: getting someone to trust the wrong download and approve a powerful permission. That gives Android users a chance to stop RatHat before it reaches the most damaging stages. Google's response adds another important piece of reassurance. The company says no apps containing RatHat are showing up on Google Play based on its detection, and Play Protect already guards Android users against known versions of the malware.

Still, that protection works best when you avoid sideloading questionable apps and pay close attention to powerful permission requests. Keep Play Protect running and add strong antivirus protection to your phone. Wireless Debugging should stay off unless you know exactly why you need it. If RatHat does make it onto a device, do not assume deleting the app solves the problem. A confirmed infection calls for a much more serious cleanup.
Does knowing AI-powered malware like RatHat can quietly take control of your phone make you think twice about installing apps outside Google Play? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Fox News AI Newsletter: The neighborhood on the edge of America's tech frontier
summary: The Fox News AI Newsletter covers the latest artificial intelligence technology advancements, including the challenges and opportunities AI presents now and for the future.
story: Homeowners living just 200 feet from a data center in Loudoun County, Virginia, describe life next to America’s AI boom.

PARTY CRASHERS: Protesters crashed a large pro-data center party in Washington, D.C., making obscene gestures at attendees and shouting about the industry's water use as President Donald Trump pushes to accelerate America's artificial intelligence and data center boom.

title: How to find compromised passwords on iPhone and Android
summary: Apple and Google password managers can flag compromised, weak and reused passwords on your phone before credential stuffing attacks can strike.
story: Google General Counsel Halimah Delaine Prado joins 'Fox & Friends' to detail how Google is fighting AI-powered phishing scams.

You probably have more passwords than you realize. Banking, email, shopping accounts and streaming services can add up quickly. The bigger problem comes when one of those passwords lands in a data leak and you have no idea it happened. Your phone may already know about it.

Both Apple and Google can check saved passwords for security problems and warn you when a login appears compromised. Apple can also flag passwords that are weak or reused. Google Password Manager offers a Password Checkup that can identify compromised, reused or weak passwords. That gives you a chance to fix an exposed login before someone tries to use it against you.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare With AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK
An iPhone can warn you when a saved password appears in a known data leak and prompt you to change it. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Your phone may already know which passwords need attention

Password alerts are one of those security features that can quietly sit on your phone until you actually open them. When you do, you might be surprised by what you find. On iPhone, Apple says the Passwords app automatically identifies common weaknesses, including passwords that are easy to guess or used multiple times. Your iPhone can also securely monitor saved passwords and warn you when they appear in known data leaks. Google Password Manager offers a similar check for credentials stored in your Google Account. Google says it can identify passwords that were exposed, are weak or are being used across multiple accounts. Checking only takes a minute.
How to find compromised passwords on iPhone
On an iPhone running iOS 27:

Open the Passwords app.Authenticate with Face ID, Touch ID or your passcode if prompted.Tap Security.Review any accounts that Apple has flagged.Tap an account to see why Apple recommends changing the password.Tap Change Password and update the password on the website or in the app.
Open the Passwords app.
Authenticate with Face ID, Touch ID or your passcode if prompted.
Tap Security.
Review any accounts that Apple has flagged.
Tap an account to see why Apple recommends changing the password.
Tap Change Password and update the password on the website or in the app.

Apple may flag a login because the password appeared in a known data leak. You can also see recommendations for passwords that are weak or reused. If the website supports it, you may also be able to switch to a passkey or upgrade to Sign in with Apple. Otherwise, your iPhone can help create a strong replacement password for many accounts.
Make sure compromised password detection is turned on
While you are checking your passwords, make sure the monitoring feature itself is enabled.
On iOS 27:
Open Settings.Tap Apps.Tap Passwords.Make sure Detect Compromised Passwords is turned on.
Open Settings.
Tap Apps.
Tap Passwords.
Make sure Detect Compromised Passwords is turned on.

Apple confirms that this setting allows the iPhone to monitor saved passwords and warn you when they appear in known data leaks. It is an easy setting to overlook, and I would rather have my phone warn me than discover an exposed password after someone has already tried to use it.
GOOGLE DOCS PASSWORD LEAK REVEALS A COSTLY SECURITY MISTAKE
Google Password Manager’s Password Checkup can flag compromised, reused and weak passwords saved to your Google Account. (Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images)
How to find compromised passwords on Samsung Galaxy

These steps are based on the latest Samsung One UI 9 software, which is built on Android 17. Samsung began its broader One UI 9 rollout in September 2026, although availability varies by phone model, carrier and region. Galaxy phones can save login information with Google Password Manager, Samsung Pass or another password manager. If your passwords are saved with Google, the most reliable way to check them for security problems is through Chrome.
To check passwords saved with Google Password Manager:
Open Chrome.Tap the three-dot menu.Tap Settings.Tap Google Password Manager.Tap Checkup.Review any passwords flagged as compromised, reused or weak.
Open Chrome.
Tap the three-dot menu.
Tap Settings.
Tap Google Password Manager.
Tap Checkup.
Review any passwords flagged as compromised, reused or weak.
Google Password Manager can identify passwords that were exposed in a data breach. It can also flag passwords that are weak or used for more than one account.

If you use Samsung Pass instead, keep in mind that Samsung documents it as a service for storing and autofilling login information using biometric authentication. Samsung Pass is also integrated with Samsung Wallet on supported Galaxy devices. Samsung does not currently document the same compromised-password checking feature that Google provides through Password Checkup.

To review login information stored with Samsung Pass, open Samsung Wallet and access Samsung Pass. If you want active breach monitoring and password-health tools, a dedicated password manager can provide additional protection.
How to find compromised passwords on Google Pixel

These steps are based on Android 17 with the latest September 2026 Pixel software. Google began rolling out its September 2026 Pixel update to supported Android 17 devices on September 15, with availability varying by carrier and device. On current Pixel phones, look for the Passwords app. Google says this app provides a shortcut to Google Password Manager, where you can access passwords and passkeys saved to your Google Account.
To check for compromised passwords, the most consistently documented route is through Chrome:

Open Chrome.Tap the three-dot menu.Tap Settings.Tap Google Password Manager.Tap Checkup.Review any passwords flagged as compromised, reused or weak.Select a flagged account and follow the prompts to change the password.
Open Chrome.
Tap the three-dot menu.
Tap Settings.
Tap Google Password Manager.
Tap Checkup.
Review any passwords flagged as compromised, reused or weak.
Select a flagged account and follow the prompts to change the password.

You can also open the Passwords app to quickly access Google Password Manager. If you do not see the app, open Settings, search for Password Manager and select it. Google Password Manager can warn you when saved credentials have been exposed online. It can also identify weak passwords and passwords being used for more than one account.
IDENTITY RESTORATION: WHAT TO DO AFTER IDENTITY THEFT
Turning on the detect compromised passwords setting lets your iPhone monitor saved logins and alert you when one may have been exposed. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What does a compromised password warning actually mean?

Seeing the word compromised can make your stomach drop. However, the warning does not automatically mean someone has already logged into your account. Apple can alert you when a password appears in a known data leak. Google can warn you when one of your saved passwords has been published online or otherwise identified as compromised.

Either way, I would take the warning seriously. An exposed password may already be available to criminals even if nobody has successfully used it against your account yet. One risk is credential stuffing. Criminals take usernames and passwords obtained from previous breaches and try the same combinations on other services. That is why reusing a password can turn one exposed login into a much bigger headache.
What to do when your phone flags a password

Start by going directly to the company's official website or app and changing the password there. Avoid using a password-reset link from an unexpected email or text. Criminals know breach warnings get your attention, and phishing messages can use that fear against you.

Next, check whether you used the same password somewhere else. If you did, change it on those accounts too. Each important account should have its own strong password so one exposed login cannot easily be reused somewhere else.

Then, add two-factor authentication (2FA) when the account supports it. We recommend turning on 2-Step Verification for stronger protection of your saved sign-in information. You should also consider passkeys when they are available. Passkeys can replace traditional passwords on supported accounts and are designed to provide stronger protection against phishing.
When a dedicated password manager may make more sense

Apple Passwords and Google Password Manager are convenient, especially if most of your devices live inside one ecosystem. However, plenty of us bounce between an iPhone, a Windows PC, a Mac or different browsers during the day. That is where a dedicated password manager can become especially useful.

A dedicated password manager can keep one encrypted vault synced across multiple devices and platforms. Many also work with major browsers, so your logins can follow you when you switch between computers, phones and tablets. Features such as autofill and password generation can also make it easier to use a different strong password for every account.

Some password managers add security tools that can flag weak or reused passwords and alert you when saved credentials may have appeared in a breach. For someone with dozens or even hundreds of logins, that gives you one central place to generate passwords, store them and keep an eye on their security.
Check out the best expert-reviewed password managers of 2026 at Cyberguy.com.
Pay extra attention to your most important accounts

If your password check produces a long list of warnings, you do not need to panic and change everything at once. I would start with your primary email account. Password-reset links for many of your other accounts probably land there, making email an especially valuable target. Then deal with financial accounts, your Apple or Google account and services holding sensitive personal information. After that, work through the rest of the warnings. If you find an account you abandoned years ago and no longer need, consider closing it instead of leaving another forgotten login sitting online.
Reused passwords can turn one breach into a much bigger problem

Suppose a small website you joined years ago suffers a breach. You may barely remember creating the account. If that old password matches one you still use somewhere important, criminals now have a combination they can try somewhere else. Using the same password on multiple accounts raises your risk if one of those passwords gets stolen. This is one reason a password manager can help. You do not have to come up with a memorable variation every time you create an account. The manager can generate a unique password and remember it for you.
Do not ignore the alerts after you clean everything up

Running a password check once is helpful, but leave the monitoring features enabled afterward. Apple can continue watching saved passwords for appearances in known leaks. Google Password Manager also continues checking passwords and can notify you when saved credentials are found online. Google even allows you to control its password alerts from Password Manager settings. That turns your password manager into an early-warning system rather than something you only open after a breach makes the news.
Kurt's key takeaways

What I like about these password checks is that they do some of the detective work for you. You do not have to remember every company that suffered a breach or wonder whether an old password is still floating around online. Your phone or password manager can flag trouble and give you a chance to deal with it. I would start by checking the passwords already saved on your phone. Fix anything marked compromised, pay close attention to reused passwords and leave the alerts turned on afterward. If you move between several devices or want more security tools in one place, a dedicated password manager can also make the whole process easier to manage.
When was the last time you checked your saved passwords for security warnings, and how many compromised or reused passwords do you think you would find? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Ithaca council halts Cornell event permits amid scrutiny over handling of rape allegations
summary: Ithaca Common Council voted 9-1 to block Cornell University permits over the school's handling of Jane Doe's rape allegations against fraternity members.
story: Ithaca Mayor Robert G. Cantelmo announced Wednesday that the city council had approved a moratorium on city permits to Cornell University and affiliated student groups. (City of Ithaca)

The Ithaca Common Council voted late Wednesday night to stop issuing city permits to Cornell University and affiliated student groups, including fraternities, following widespread criticism of the Ivy League school's handling of rape allegations made by a former student.

After hours of debate, the council voted 9-1 in favor of a moratorium, which temporarily bars Cornell from obtaining new permits for assemblies, parades and special events at the Ithaca Commons and activities requiring noise permits, citing public safety concerns.

The measure drew support from numerous Cornell students and Ithaca residents, although some graduate students raised concerns that the restrictions were overly broad and could disrupt activities unrelated to Greek life.

The fraternity house at the center of a rape allegation by a former Cornell student identified as "Jane Doe" stands on the campus of Cornell University on October 7, 2026, in Ithaca, New York. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)
CORNELL PROTESTERS SWARM CAMPUS TO SUPPORT JANE DOE, CALL FOR UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT'S RESIGNATION
One graduate student warned that the moratorium could result in canceled or delayed events, lost deposits, reduced access to venues and disruptions to conferences.

The moratorium will stay in place until Nov. 5, unless the council extends it at a later date. The measure also includes an amendment that requires Cornell to refer investigations involving sexual and violent crimes to the Ithaca Police Department, though its unclear how that will be enforced.

The moratorium comes after the student, identified as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit in September accusing seven former Chi Phi fraternity members of drugging and raping her on the night of Oct. 19, 2024, and into the following morning.

In the lawsuit, she alleges she arrived at the frat house already intoxicated, after which the men pressured her into taking ketamine and other substances. The men have denied wrongdoing, with some maintaining the sexual activity was consensual and others denying they participated.
Students protest on Ho Plaza at Cornell University, Monday, October 5, 2026, in Ithaca, New York, in response to an alleged sexual assault in 2024. (Richard Beetham for Fox News Digital)
CORNELL PICKS FORMER DEPUTY US ATTORNEY GENERAL TO REVIEW SEX ASSAULT RESPONSE
The fraternity was suspended on Nov. 8, 2024, the same day Doe reported sexual assault allegations to campus police, according to Doe's civil complaint.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who initially declined to pursue charges, has said Doe's Nov. 2024 sworn statement did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang-raped and, instead, described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as "voluntary, conscious, and consensual."

However, CBS New York obtained the transcript of the Cornell police interviews with Jane Doe on Nov. 14 and 15, 2024, during which she told investigators: "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."

Van Houten said he was never provided the full transcript. Late last month, he announced his office was reopening the case because the allegations contained in Jane Doe's lawsuit differed from her sworn statement nearly two years earlier.

Thousands of Cornell University students and others from the Cornell community fill Ho Plaza for the Justice for Survivors protest hosted by 20 student organizations Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. (Matt Burkhartt/For The Washington Post via Getty Images)
BAR NAMED IN CORNELL RAPE LAWSUIT DISPUTES ACCUSER'S ACCOUNT, SAYS SHE WAS NEVER SERVED ALCOHOL WHILE UNDERAGE

In an interview with The Associated Press on Wednesday, Jane Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said Cornell police led her to believe the criminal investigation remained active even though Van Houten had decided against filing charges just days after she first spoke with investigators.
Van Houten has said he instructed Cornell police to inform Jane Doe that charges would not be pursued, but acknowledged he never spoke directly with her or her attorney.
Gov. Kathy Hochul effectively took the investigation out of Van Houten's hands on Oct. 1, by appointing Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor on the case.

"Newly released information continues to raise serious questions about the investigation conducted by the Cornell Police Department and the decision by the Tompkins County District Attorney not to prosecute an alleged sexual assault on Cornell University's campus in October 2024," Hochul said in a statement.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James during a news conference in New York on Oct. 2, 2026. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
She added: "This has, in turn, undercut my faith, and the public's faith, in the District Attorney's ability to effectively investigate and prosecute the case at this time."

On Wednesday, one of the men named in Jane Doe's lawsuit petitioned a court to remove James from the case, accusing her of bias over a social media post she made days before her appointment in which she called what Doe allegedly endured "horrific and unacceptable," The Associated Press reported.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: California woman accused of spying for China fights detention with $820K in proposed security
summary: Wanying Zhang offered over $800,000 in property equity for bail after her arrest while boarding a flight to China on unregistered agent charges.
story: Central District of California U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli criticizes Democratic senators for blocking a fraud bill and discusses the recent arrest of a woman for allegedly spying on behalf of China on ‘The Big Weekend Show.’

A California real estate agent accused of gathering intelligence on a relative of Taiwan's president for the Chinese government sought release from federal custody Wednesday, offering more than $800,000 in property equity and financial guarantees while disputing prosecutors' claims that she posed a flight risk.

Wanying Zhang, 34, of Irvine, argued through her attorney that her American citizenship, family ties and history of returning from overseas trips demonstrated she would appear for future court proceedings, according to a nine-page defense filing obtained by Fox News Digital.
Zhang was arrested Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport while preparing to board a flight to China. She faces a federal charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.
FEDS SAY US CITIZEN GATHERED INFORMATION ON AMERICAN TARGETS FOR CHINESE COMMUNIST PARTY
This photo provided by the Federal Bureau of Investigation shows Wanying Zhang being arrested Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026, in Los Angeles. (Federal Bureau of Investigation via AP)
Her attorney, Craig Harbaugh, told the court that Zhang came to the United States in 2014, became a naturalized citizen in 2020 and has worked in Orange County real estate for approximately a decade.
She lives with her husband and their two daughters, ages 8 and 5, according to the filing.

The defense proposed using an Irvine residence with at least $700,000 in equity to secure her release, along with $120,000 in financial guarantees from her husband, his sister, his father and a family friend.
This undated photo released by the U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, shows Wanying Zhang. (U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California via AP)
Harbaugh also proposed GPS-monitored home detention, surrendering travel documents, electronic-device monitoring and restrictions on entering airports or contacting individuals connected to the case.

The defense acknowledged that Pretrial Services recommended detention over concerns about Zhang's potential failure to appear in court, but argued that strict release conditions would adequately address those concerns.
Zhang's lawyers also disputed the significance of her one-way ticket to China, arguing that she frequently booked international trips using separately purchased outbound and return flights.
According to the filing, Zhang had traveled to China, France and Japan during the past year and returned to the United States after each trip.
The defense said her planned October trip was intended to visit her mother and had been postponed until after her daughters' birthdays.
TAIWAN ANALYSTS SAY TRUMP-XI SUMMIT PRODUCED NO POLICY SHIFT BUT REAL TEST LIES AHEAD
The underlying criminal complaint alleges Zhang participated in a September 2025 surveillance operation outside the Seattle-area residence of a close relative of a Taiwanese government official.
According to an FBI affidavit, investigators reviewed security-camera footage allegedly showing Zhang and another individual photographing the person and family members near their home.
Travelers exit a terminal at Los Angeles International Airport on Monday, March 23, 2026, in Los Angeles. (Ethan Swope/AP Photo)
Federal authorities also alleged that Zhang transmitted photographs, video and vehicle information to a suspected Chinese government official through electronic communications.
Investigators said Zhang attended China's University of International Relations in Beijing, which the FBI described as closely associated with China's intelligence apparatus.
Zhang's attorneys contest the charge and maintain that she intends to establish her innocence.

She faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in federal prison if convicted.

title: Washington jewelry store owner opens fire after would-be thieves ram truck through storefront

story: A Washington jewelry store owner opened fire on a group of masked would-be thieves after they rammed a pickup truck through his storefront in broad daylight and rushed inside, sending the suspects scrambling from the store empty-handed, authorities said. (Credit: Lynnwood Police Department)

Masked would-be thieves smashed a pickup truck through the front of a Washington jewelry store in broad daylight and stormed inside — only to be sent scrambling when the store owner pulled a gun and opened fire, according to authorities and a local report.
The attempted robbery unfolded shortly after 12:25 p.m. on Tuesday at Medina Jewelers in Lynnwood.
Surveillance video shows three vehicles circling the parking lot before a white Toyota Tacoma barrels through the storefront, shattering glass and sending employees running.

Surveillance video shows three vehicles circling the parking lot before a white Toyota Tacoma barrels through the storefront, shattering glass and sending employees running. (Lynnwood Police Department)
Several masked suspects then rush through the opening, including one who appears to be carrying an axe.
The store owner grabbed a gun and fired, sending the group fleeing empty-handed, according to FOX13 Seattle.
Several masked suspects then rush through the opening, including one who appears to be carrying an axe. (Lynnwood Police Department)
No injuries were reported at the scene, though police said it was unclear whether any of the suspects had been struck by gunfire.
REPEAT OFFENDER BUSTED AGAIN LESS THAN 24 HOURS AFTER RELEASE IN BRAZEN JEWELRY STORE THEFT CASE: POLICE
"It was broad daylight and a pretty rare occurrence for us," Lynnwood Police Cmdr. Joe Dickenson told the outlet.
A man, who is reported to be the store owner, is seen pointing a gun at the suspects as they flee the scene. (Lynnwood Police Department)
Police were still working to determine whether any of the suspects had a firearm.
"You had several witnesses that were out and about, several pedestrians walking around; all of a sudden, a car crashing into a building and shots ringing out is cause for alarm," Dickenson said.
The suspects escaped in a black BMW SUV and a silver Toyota or Infiniti sedan, police said. The BMW struck a parked vehicle while fleeing and may have damage to its front passenger side.

title: Colorado police sergeant reveals how human traffickers target vulnerable children: ‘Happening in our backyard’
summary: The Aurora Police Department Human Trafficking Unit recovered 29 survivors, including 15 minors, in its first year by targeting exploitation of vulnerable youth.
story: Sgt. Joseph Sullivan shares a teenage trafficking victim’s devastating plea and explains how the Aurora, Colorado, police department’s dedicated unit recovered 29 survivors, including 15 minors, and arrested 28 suspects in its first year.

Human traffickers are turning children’s hunger, desperation and need for affection into tools of exploitation, a Colorado city police sergeant warned after his dedicated unit’s first year brought dozens of survivors to safety.
The Aurora Police Department (APD) Human Trafficking Unit opened 53 investigations, arrested 28 suspects and recovered 29 survivors, including 15 minors, in its first year.
APD Sgt. Joseph Sullivan told Fox News Digital the work is exposing abuse that residents may never suspect is happening around them.
According to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), "human trafficking involves the use of force, fraud, or coercion to obtain some type of labor or commercial sex act."
MIKE WALTZ, TIM TEBOW LAUNCH EFFORT TO COMBAT ONLINE CHILD EXPLOITATION: 'IT'S HAPPENING IN THEIR BACKYARD'
Federal law enforcement reported 36 truck-stop-based instances of human trafficking in 2023, according to the National Human Trafficking Hotline. (iStock)
"It is happening in our backyard, not just in those other places," Sullivan said.
For Sullivan, one teenage girl’s plea captures both the urgency of that mission and the difficult road survivors face after investigators reach them.
The 16-year-old had been brought to Aurora — a city of just over 400,000 people outside Denver — from another town by her boyfriend, who then left her there, Sullivan said.
Trying to survive, she was sexually exploited by people around an apartment complex in exchange for somewhere to stay, drugs or food.
SIX UNDERAGE GIRLS RECOVERED IN SWEEPING OPERATION TARGETING NOTORIOUS TRAFFICKING CORRIDOR

People hold signs calling for an end to human trafficking. Aurora police’s dedicated Human Trafficking Unit recovered 29 survivors, including 15 minors, in its first year. (Stephen Maturen/Getty Images, File)
During an interview, she asked a detective to find those responsible.
"'I really hope that you can find the people that are doing this, because it really hurts what I’m having to do just to survive,'" Sullivan recalled her saying.
The girl died of an overdose a few months later, he said.
Her words stayed with him.
"It really is satisfying being able to contact these survivors and then identify who’s exploiting them and holding them accountable," Sullivan said.
FLORIDA-LED OPERATION RESCUES 163 CHILDREN AROUND GLOBE IN HISTORIC STATE SWEEP, HUNTS SUSPECTED PREDATORS
The Aurora police trafficking unit has three detectives and a supervising sergeant. (Fox News Digital, File)
But reaching someone does not guarantee an immediate or lasting escape. Survivors may need repeated contact, resources and offers of help before they can find a way out, he said.
That is part of why having dedicated detectives matters.

Created in September 2025, the trafficking unit has three detectives and a supervising sergeant. Sullivan said its focus is sex trafficking involving people 21 and younger, allowing the small team to concentrate its efforts.
The investigations demand time to gather evidence, build cases and help victims feel comfortable enough to testify.
"Having a dedicated unit helps lower their overall caseload and allows them to apply the time and effort that these cases deserve," Sullivan said.
DOJ SAYS 11 MIGRANTS INDICTED IN MULTI-STATE SEX TRAFFICKING, DRUG, FIREARMS CASE
APD Investigations Bureau Cmdr. Marc Paolino said the unit was built to put survivors at the center of investigations while targeting those exploiting them.

"The work they’ve done has made our community safer and sent a clear message that the Aurora Police Department will aggressively pursue anyone who exploits others for this type of heinous, criminal activity," Paolino said in a department release.
Among those arrested is Marshae Wheelock, 24, of Aurora, whom police linked to multiple cases allegedly involving the exploitation of children over several years.

"Marshae Wheelock represents the type of offender the Human Trafficking Unit was created to investigate; someone who repeatedly preys on vulnerable children," APD Deputy Chief Mark Hildebrand said in the release.
TRUMP SIGNS HAWLEY MEASURE ADDING 200 CHILD EXPLOITATION INVESTIGATORS IN LARGEST CRACKDOWN EFFORT YET
The Aurora Police Department works with human services officials, nonprofit organizations and victim advocates. (Aurora Police Department)

The department also detailed a February undercover operation in which investigators recovered a 16-year-old girl and later identified three suspects accused of sexually exploiting her for financial gain.

Sullivan cautioned that trafficking often looks very different from the abductions portrayed in movies. Someone does not have to be snatched off the street by another person to exploit their vulnerability.
"There is some kind of need that a trafficker identifies to exploit, and that’s how they get in," Sullivan said.
That need could be housing, food, money or affection. Filling it through legitimate support is a central part of helping survivors, he said.

The APD works with human services officials, nonprofit organizations and victim advocates. Sullivan pointed to a local group, From Silence to Saved, which helps victims from the beginning of an investigation through court proceedings and afterward.
MORE THAN 300 ARRESTED IN SPRAWLING CALIFORNIA CRACKDOWN ON CHILD EXPLOITATION CRIMES

Callahan Walsh of the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children warns that financial sextortion targeting teenage boys has reached unprecedented levels since COVID with devastating consequences. (Stepheny Price/Fox News Digital)
He also credited support from police leadership and organizations that provide tools to help detectives identify victims online.
Sullivan oversees Aurora’s Internet Crimes Against Children team, as well as its trafficking detectives. The teams investigate distinct crimes, including sextortion, but their work can overlap.
The department said the trafficking unit draws on local, state and federal partnerships, and investigative resources through the Colorado Cyber Guardian Task Force.
The threats also cross geographic and economic boundaries.
Asked whether Tren de Aragua (TdA) had been involved in the trafficking his team investigated, Sullivan said his unit had not encountered that connection.
His broader point was that exploitation can affect people across backgrounds.

Sullivan described another high school student who came from a wealthier background but became vulnerable after her mother suffered a disabling medical crisis and her father was absent. The girl became addicted to drugs and was exploited by someone else, he said.
FBI AND TEXAS AUTHORITIES ARREST 276 SUSPECTED CHILD PREDATORS, RESCUE 89 CHILDREN IN SWEEPING OPERATION
"There really is no boundary on where we see victims," Sullivan said.
Investigators regularly work with other agencies, including when victims travel between states.
"This is a problem in every community around the country, whether it’s a big city or small," he added.
For parents, Sullivan’s advice begins with staying involved and asking questions about what their children are doing online.

Warning signs can include unexplained cash, new clothes or paid-for manicures, as well as disappearing for a weekend and returning with things they did not have before. He encouraged families to use educational resources from the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children.

Some investigations remain stalled while detectives await additional information, Sullivan said. Survivors may not be ready to come forward or may not recognize themselves as victims, making it harder to advance a case.
A human trafficking bust in Florida resulted in the arrests of 228 individuals. (Polk County Sheriff's Office)
As the unit enters its second year, its priorities remain identifying victims and building cases against those exploiting them.
Public tips can help detectives reach people sooner, he said.
"We don’t turn away any kind of tips," Sullivan said.

He also urged people experiencing exploitation to seek support even if they are not ready to participate in a criminal investigation. Advocacy organizations can help without involving police, he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
For the detectives, the mission continues beyond an arrest: working with partners to meet the needs traffickers used to gain control in the first place.
"Using a group of people to help identify those needs and provide those needs is kind of the goal and the key to us being successful," Sullivan said.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Former corrections officer accused of killing wife, forcing kids to help
summary: A former corrections officer allegedly strangled his wife and forced some of his children to help during the attack, then hid her body in a dumpster.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A former Missouri probation and parole officer who later worked at a state correctional center allegedly killed his wife in front of some of his children, even making some of the youngsters help him abuse their mother.

Jonathan G. Houston, 44, was arrested after one of his children called 911 from a hotel and discreetly whispered to dispatchers that her father had "captured" her and her six siblings and had physically abused them for years, according to charging documents, KOMU reported.
Deputies responded to the report and found the children on Sunday at the Baymont Inn & Suites in Kingdom City.
MISSOURI ASSISTANT FIRE CHIEF CHARGED WITH MURDER AFTER HIDDEN VIDEO FOUND ON WIFE'S PHONE, INVESTIGATORS SAY
Jonathan G. Houston, 44, was charged with first-degree murder and first-degree kidnapping. (Callaway County Sheriff's Office)

One of the children told the deputies that their father had strangled their mother while some of the children were present 10 months earlier, according to the documents. Another child, who also recalled witnessing the strangulation, said her father told her he planned to kill her mother, who was later identified by deputies as 37-year-old Aunika C. Houston.

During that attack, Houston was allegedly gripping his wife by the throat when he forced one child to pour hot water down the woman's legs and another child to cover her mouth to muffle her screams, the documents show.

Houston had locked his three youngest children in the bathroom and instructed the children in the room to play loud music, so others could not hear their mother's screams, according to court records, KOMU reported.
The man allegedly put his wife’s body in a trash bag and threw it into a dumpster on the hotel's property.
KANSAS CONVICTED FELON, SEX OFFENDER ALLEGEDLY KILLS FELLOW FAMILY MEMBERS BEFORE TAKING HIS OWN LIFE: POLICE
The man allegedly put his wife’s body in a trash bag and threw it into a dumpster on the hotel's property. (Callaway County Sheriff's Office)
The woman was never reported missing after the killing.

"Aunika Houston was originally from the State of California and is believed to have been residing in the Central Missouri area for the past several years. Her next of kin has been notified," the Callaway County Sheriff’s Office said in a press release.
Houston allegedly admitted to investigators that he killed his wife and had planned the killing in advance, according to the charging documents.

"There is no danger to the community. This seems to be an act of domestic violence, and it's very unfortunate for everybody involved," Callaway County Sheriff’s Office Chief Deputy Curtis Hall told KOMU.
The woman was never reported missing after the killing. (Callaway County Sheriff's Office)

title: Texas executes Jamaal Howard despite concerns over lethal injection drug used in failed Tennessee execution
summary: Jamaal Howard's attorneys cited Christa Pike's failed lethal injection in Tennessee to argue the pentobarbital drug posed risks, but the Supreme Court rejected it.
story: Christa Pike asked "Where am I?" and "Who are you?" after unexpectedly waking up Tuesday following a botched lethal injection last week, according to her attorney Randy Spivey. He said her team had believed she was "brain dead" before she awoke.

A Texas man convicted of killing a convenience store clerk during a robbery was executed Wednesday evening after the Supreme Court declined to halt the execution, despite his attorneys raising concerns about the lethal injection drug used in a failed execution attempt in Tennessee last week.
Jamaal Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8:03 p.m. He was sentenced to death for the 2000 killing of 42-year-old Vickie Swartout in Silsbee, Texas.

Prior to Howard's execution, his attorneys pointed to the failed execution of Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital on Sept. 30, arguing that the same drug Texas planned to use could pose similar risks.
"Texas should not be eager to follow in Tennessee’s footsteps; a stay would keep that from happening," Howard's attorneys argued in their filing.
CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEYS SAY SHE'S IN CRITICAL CONDITION AFTER BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTIONS

The U.S. Supreme Court declined to halt Jamaal Howard's execution after his attorneys raised concerns about the lethal injection drug used by Texas. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice; AP Photo/Pat Sullivan)
The Supreme Court rejected Howard's emergency appeal without explanation. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice to publicly dissent, Fox News reported.
The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals had previously rejected two requests to stop the execution based on concerns about the drug's use.
According to The Associated Press, as the pentobarbital began taking effect Wednesday evening, Howard took a couple of breaths and gasped.

Howard then began making snoring sounds, coughed and resumed the snoring sounds, which grew progressively quieter. His movements reportedly stopped entirely after around 30 seconds, and he was pronounced dead 19 minutes later.
CHRISTA PIKE’S BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTION TAKES FOCUS OFF VICTIM, JEOPARDIZES EXECUTION: FORMER POLICE CHIEF
Jamaal Howard, 46, was executed in Texas on Oct. 7, 2026, for the 2000 killing of convenience store clerk Vickie Swartout. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice)
Howard's attorneys also said in court filings that they had requested information about the dose of pentobarbital the Texas Department of Criminal Justice planned to use to carry out the execution.
The concerns stemmed in part from Pike's execution attempt, during which she reportedly survived two doses of pentobarbital.

Howard's execution took place the same day a Tennessee judge granted a request from Pike's attorneys to order the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence connected to the failed execution attempt.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Pike is the first person to survive a lethal injection in the modern era.
CHRISTA PIKE EXECUTION FAILURE SPARES MURDERER WHO BAILED VICTIM OUT JUST TO KILL HIM

Randy Spivey, an attorney for Christa Pike, a death row prisoner who survived a botched execution, speaks to the media, flanked by Luke Ihnen, after a Tennessee court was presented a status update on Pike, outside a courtroom in Nashville, Tennessee, Oct. 7, 2026. (Reuters/Seth Herald)

Howard's attorneys also argued before the Supreme Court that his execution should be halted because he was intellectually disabled. However, the state said his attorneys had not presented evidence establishing that he met the legal criteria for intellectual disability.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Howard was convicted of capital murder in the killing of Swartout, who was shot once in the chest during a convenience store robbery.
Howard, who was 20 years old at the time, also took $114 from the cash register during the robbery.
Fox News Digital's Michael Ruiz and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

story: Fox News correspondent Brooke Taylor reports on U.S. military recruitment achievements under the Trump administration on ‘Special Report.’

FIRST ON FOX: The U.S. Coast Guard recruited its largest enlisted class in nearly four decades during fiscal year 2026, surpassing its recruiting goals for the third consecutive year as the service works to expand its ranks.
According to the Coast Guard, 5,445 active-duty members enlisted in fiscal year 2026, up from 5,204 in 2025 and 4,422 in 2024.
The service also commissioned 346 active-duty officers, the second-highest total in its history.
"These record-breaking recruitment numbers prove that the call to serve still resonates deeply across our country," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement.
US ARMY HITS 2026 RECRUITING GOALS FOUR MONTHS EARLY, PETE HEGSETH ANNOUNCES AT WEST POINT COMMENCEMENT
The U.S. Coast Guard enlisted 5,445 active-duty recruits in fiscal year 2026, marking its largest recruiting class in nearly four decades. (U.S. Coast Guard)

"I am incredibly proud to stand beside these new Coast Guard men and women who have stepped up to defend our homeland," he continued. "They represent the very best of who we are, and we are going to make sure they have the tools, the training and the support to get the job done."
During fiscal year 2026, the Coast Guard expanded its recruiting efforts, opening four recruiting offices in Miami, Florida; Long Island, New York; Austin, Texas; and the Netherlands.
Coast Guard Vice Commandant Adm. Tom Allan said the numbers reflect growing interest in serving.
COAST GUARD ENDING RACE-BASED ADMISSIONS FOR OFFICER COMMISSIONING PROGRAM UNDER TRUMP DEI CRACKDOWN
The U.S. Coast Guard surpassed its recruiting goals for the third consecutive year in fiscal year 2026. (U.S. Coast Guard)
"We surpassed our recruiting goals because Americans are ready and willing to serve in the U.S. Coast Guard, conducting exciting missions that deliver results our Nation needs," Allan said.

"This momentum is about more than numbers; it is about being the world’s best Coast Guard and building the workforce America needs," he added. "We are proud to welcome our newest members and grateful to our recruiters for continuing to deliver exceptional results."
The service is also investing in new infrastructure to help train its expanding workforce.
The Coast Guard awarded a $400 million contract to modernize Training Center Cape May in New Jersey, marking the largest shore construction award in the service's history.

The facility serves as the Coast Guard's sole basic training center for enlisted recruits, and the improvements are intended to accommodate its growing workforce.
The recruitment gains come as the Coast Guard pursues a modernization initiative known as Force Design.

title: Driver opens fire on strangers along major US interstate, tells cops he ‘had to kill people today’
summary: Andrew Darrick Tanaka allegedly told police, "I had to kill people today," after allegedly opening fire on vehicles along Interstate 35 in Warren County.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
An Iowa man accused of opening fire on passing vehicles along an interstate and wounding a woman allegedly made a chilling admission to police after his arrest, according to court documents.

Andrew Darrick Tanaka, 27, of West Des Moines, faces four counts of attempted murder in Monday afternoon's shootings along Interstate 35 in Warren County, according to the Iowa Department of Public Safety.
After being taken into custody, Tanaka allegedly told law enforcement, "I had to kill people today," according to a criminal complaint and affidavit filed Tuesday in Warren County District Court.

The incident began around 3:31 p.m. Monday when authorities received multiple 911 calls reporting gunfire along the northbound lanes of I-35.VIDEO SHOWS IOWA ROAD RAGE SUSPECT SURRENDER AFTER POLICE ORDER HIM TO DROP GUN
Andrew Darrick Tanaka, 27, faces four counts of attempted murder after allegedly opening fire on multiple vehicles along Interstate 35 in Iowa Oct. 5, 2026. (Iowa Department of Public Safety)
Tanaka was driving a black Chevrolet Equinox when a woman driving a black BMW passed him on the interstate, according to the affidavit. The BMW then passed a Subaru Outback.
Investigators allege Tanaka caught up to the Subaru and fired at least two rounds through the driver's side window, striking the woman behind the wheel in her left shoulder.
He then allegedly caught up to the BMW and fired another round through its driver's side window.

Tanaka continued north before rear-ending a gray Nissan Altima carrying two people, according to the affidavit.APPARENT ROAD RAGE DRIVER APPEARS TO THREATEN MOM ON CAMERA AS 3-YEAR-OLD CRIES IN BACK SEAT
Authorities have not disclosed a motive for the shootings along Interstate 35 in Iowa. (Stephen M. Katz/South Florida Sun-Sentinel/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
When the Nissan's occupants stopped to check on him, Tanaka allegedly got out of his vehicle with a handgun and fired at least one round into the car's windshield.
Deputies from the Warren County Sheriff's Office, officers from the West Des Moines Police Department and Iowa State Patrol troopers responded to reports of gunfire near mile marker 56.

Officers found the wounded woman and several vehicles that appeared to have been struck by gunfire. The woman was taken to a hospital with injuries that authorities said did not appear to be life-threatening.
Police later found Tanaka along the interstate after his vehicle became disabled after the collision.POLICE SWARM MICHIGAN SHOPPING CENTER AFTER 'SIGNIFICANT' SHOOTING INCIDENT; AT LEAST 2 DEAD
The Des Moines skyline as seen from the lookout at Two Rivers Park Oct. 9, 2025, in Des Moines, Iowa. (Cody Scanlan/The Register/USA Today Network via Imagn Images)
He was standing on the shoulder of the highway holding a handgun when officers arrived, according to the affidavit. Tanaka was taken into custody without further incident.
The shootings prompted authorities to shut down the interstate for several hours while investigators processed the scene.
Tanaka was booked into the Warren County Jail on four counts of attempted murder.

The Warren County Sheriff's Office and Iowa Division of Criminal Investigation are investigating the shootings.

title: Mom dies shielding baby in horrific 15-story Bronx fall as police hunt suspect: report
summary: Angel Carrasco is wanted after Nathaly Ramirez, 23, was allegedly pushed from a 15th-floor Bronx balcony with her baby in a suspected domestic violence attack.
story: New York City Police Department detectives are searching for Angel Carrasco after Nathaly Ramirez and her 8-month-old daughter pushed from a Bronx apartment balcony, police say. (Credit: FOX 5 New York)

A New York City mother and her baby were allegedly pushed from an apartment balcony in a deadly attack that left the woman dead and her infant daughter critically injured, police said, as detectives hunt a man wanted in connection with the case.
The NYPD identified Angel Carrasco, 31, as the man detectives are seeking after Nathaly Ramirez, 23, and her 8-month-old daughter were found outside their Bronx apartment building early Tuesday.

The pair fell from a 15th-floor balcony, according to FOX 5 NY, which reported that investigators were looking for Ramirez’s boyfriend or recent ex-boyfriend in a suspected domestic violence incident.
GEORGIA COLLEGE STUDENT MIRACULOUSLY SURVIVES 8-STORY PLUNGE AFTER METAL BENCH BREAKS HER FALL
Nathaly Ramirez, 23, was killed after she and her infant daughter were allegedly pushed from a Bronx apartment balcony. (FOX 5 New York)
Investigators believe Ramirez tightly embraced her daughter during the fall, likely cushioning the baby from the impact, ABC7 NY reported.
Neighbors described hearing a desperate plea moments before the horrifying incident.
"Please don’t do this!" Ramirez screamed, according to neighbors cited by FOX 5.

Officers responded to a 911 call at approximately 3:38 a.m. Tuesday outside 2550 Olinville Ave., where they found Ramirez and her daughter with injuries indicating a fall from an elevated position, the NYPD told Fox News Digital.
DATING-APP CHARMER ACCUSED OF MURDER AFTER HISTORY OF DOMESTIC ARRESTS INVOLVING WOMEN HE MET ONLINE
Nathaly Ramirez and her 8-month-old daughter were found outside this apartment building in the Bronx early Tuesday. Police determined both had been pushed from a balcony. (FOX 5 New York)
"Further investigation determined that both individuals had been pushed from a balcony," the department said.
Officers rushed the baby to a hospital in critical condition. Emergency medical personnel transported Ramirez to a hospital, where she was later pronounced dead.

Police identified Carrasco as wanted in connection with the incident in an update Wednesday and released an image of him. The department’s statement did not specify his relationship to Ramirez or announce any charges.

Sources told FOX 5 that the couple had a history of domestic violence and that police had been called to the apartment multiple times. A woman who lives two doors down told the outlet she had heard yelling from the apartment on numerous occasions.
MARYLAND DAD BLAMED 'SATAN' AFTER 2-MONTH-OLD DAUGHTER DIED FROM HORRIFIC HEAD TRAUMA
Angel Carrasco, 31, is wanted in connection with the incident that killed Nathaly Ramirez and critically injured her infant daughter, the NYPD said. (NYPD Crime Stoppers)
A neighbor identified only as Mike recalled an incident in January involving a man trying to force his way into Ramirez’s apartment, ABC7 reported.
"He was kicking the door down trying to get into the apartment," Mike told the station.

No arrests have been made, and the investigation remains ongoing, police said.
Anyone with information about Carrasco’s whereabouts can call Crime Stoppers at 1-800-577-TIPS, or submit a tip online at crimestoppers.nypdonline.org.

Christa Pike's lawyers believed the Tennessee death row inmate was "brain dead" and expected her to be taken off life support before she unexpectedly woke up Tuesday, nearly a week after the state failed two attempts to lethally inject her.

"To the shock of everyone, including me, including her team and including the medical team, Christa woke up and began talking," Randy Spivey, one of her attorneys, told reporters Wednesday after a court hearing in Nashville.
"I do not have an explanation for what happened between Monday night and Tuesday morning, but what we do know is that Christa has a long road to recovery," he added.

The parents of murdered Texas mother Christa Bauer Gilley, 38, have made their first public statements following their daughter's killing.
